entry.title: THREE SWINGS, THREE THUNDERBOLTS, AND THE RECORD BOOK REWRITTEN: BÁEZ HOMERS IN HIS FIRST THREE AT-BATS AT THE DAWN OF HIS CAREER — CARDINALS 8, CUBS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 39 · Sunday, the Sixteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THREE SWINGS, THREE THUNDERBOLTS, AND THE RECORD BOOK REWRITTEN: BÁEZ HOMERS IN HIS FIRST THREE AT-BATS AT THE DAWN OF HIS CAREER — CARDINALS 8, CUBS 4

Summoned from Memphis but a day before, the young outfielder greets the first pitch ever thrown to him in the major leagues with a four-hundred-and-forty-nine-foot thunderclap to dead center, adds a second homer his next time up and a third in the sixth — five runs driven in, a standing ovation from the rival faithful, and the first three-homer debut in the whole recorded history of the game

The Herald has chronicled prodigies before, but it has never had occasion to set down what Joshua Báez did at Wrigley Field on Saturday afternoon, for the sufficient reason that in the annals of more than three-and-twenty thousand major leaguers, no man had ever done it. The Cardinals' No. 3 prospect, summoned Friday from Memphis with his four-and-thirty Triple-A home runs, stepped in against the veteran left-hander Matthew Boyd with two out and a man aboard in the first, beheld a fastball at the letters — the first major-league pitch of his life — and dispatched it four hundred and forty-nine feet to dead center, the ball leaving his bat at nearly nine-and-a-hundred miles per hour. His second time up he worked a full count and ripped a changeup down the left-field line, becoming but the second man since 1900 to homer in his first two career at-bats in a single game, joining Bob Nieman of the 1951 Browns. And in the sixth, facing Boyd a third time, he drove a pitch the opposite way to right — 'I had no idea,' he confessed. 'So I just started running, and then I seen that it went over and I was like, this is insane' — and with it went where no ballplayer had gone before: three at-bats, three home runs, in his major-league debut.

By the eighth the entire premises had surrendered to the occasion. The Wrigley crowd — a rival crowd, be it remembered — stood for the rookie's fourth appearance, and the Chicago pitcher Colin Rea was obliged to cup a hand to his ear to hear the signals over the din. Báez lined out to left; the faithful applauded him anyway. 'It's just unreal,' said the young man, who finished three-for-four with five runs driven in. 'For me to not only get a hit, but hit three home runs is just crazy.' His manager Oliver Marmol, asked beforehand what excited him about the newcomer, had answered that the lad's talent 'doesn't quietly whisper — it screams at you'; afterward he ranked the spectacle with watching Pujols strike his seven-hundredth. The starter Michael McGreevy, who contributed six innings in which every run against him crossed unearned, submitted the day's driest verdict: 'I love when history gives me run support.' Boyd, who surrendered all three blows, tipped his cap in the old manner: 'He's a good hitter. He just got the better of me today.'

The supporting particulars: Burleson struck his twentieth homer and drove in two, Jordan added his second, and the eight runs stood comfortably against the reply of Conforto, whose tenth homer figured among three Chicago runs driven in. The Elias scribes note that no man had previously managed a three-homer game earlier than his tenth career contest; Báez required one. He is likewise the first Cardinal to homer upon the first pitch of his career since a pitcher named Adam Wainwright turned the trick in 2006. The ledger gives the affair consequence beyond the poetry: St. Louis, at two-and-sixty wins, stands three and a half games from the National's final wild-card chair, while the Cubs — still holders of the first chair by six full games — see the rubber match arrive this very afternoon.

News Around the League

THE VERDICT FROM TORONTO: GUERRERO TO THE CONCUSSION LIST, AND THE CANADIANS SHUFFLE THE DECK

The morning's report from Ontario, awaited since Friday's collision at third base, arrived and was grim enough: Vladimir Guerrero Jr. has been placed upon the seven-day concussion injured list. The club answered with a small mobilization — the left-hander Ricky Tiedemann recalled from Buffalo, the outfielder Daz Cameron selected to the roster — and the skipper John Schneider has installed young Charles McAdoo as the next man up, with results the card below celebrates. 'This definitely feels different than it has for a lot of the year,' Schneider said of his club's late charge, which has now brought seven victories in nine games. 'It feels pretty damn good.' The timing of the injury remains the cruelest part; the standings, as the desk observes below, have rarely been so crowded.

TEN THOUSAND VICTORIES BESIDE THE LAKE

Let the almanac record that Cleveland's franchise, in dismissing San Diego by six runs to one on Saturday, secured the ten-thousandth victory in its history — a summit previously attained, among clubs founded since 1900, only by the Red Sox and the Yankees. 'That's an unbelievable number to get to, and I'm honored to be a part of it,' said the manager Stephen Vogt, whose 2026 edition has supplied rather fewer than its share of the ten thousand — nine wins in seven-and-twenty games since the All-Star pause — but chose the occasion to play the complete brand of baseball its manager has been pleading for all month. The particulars of the milestone conquest are set down upon the card below.

THE TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-MILLION-DOLLAR MAN TAKES A SEAT

In Los Angeles, the management has prescribed rest for Kyle Tucker, the winter's grandest acquisition, who sat Saturday against Milwaukee — his second benching of the week at home. The affliction is geographic and stark: upon the road the man bats .275 with his customary production, but at Dodger Stadium the figure reads .192 with but two home runs in nine-and-fifty games. 'The splits are stark. I don't think we have a reason behind it,' admitted the skipper Dave Roberts, who observed frustration accumulating in a player famous for showing none. Tucker is promised a return to the lineup this day and all three games at Denver besides; his replacement Alex Call, it must be said, delivered two of the club's five hits in the losing cause.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: SKENES HELD BACK, JUDGE PLAYS CATCH, AND DEGROM AWAITS HIS VERDICT

The gravest entry first: Pittsburgh has pushed Paul Skenes from this day's assignment back to Wednesday against Detroit, the management citing rest for a young arm whose fastball has receded from 98.2 miles per hour last season to 96.8 this — though the man himself pleads ordinary weariness rather than injury. 'Everybody's tired. Everybody's grinding, and we just got to keep going,' said Skenes. In the Bronx ledger: Aaron Judge, fractured rib and all, played catch Friday for the first time since the injury, though the bat stays holstered. In Texas they exhale cautiously over Jacob deGrom, whose early exit with triceps fatigue produced an encouraging examination, though his next turn is accounted unlikely. The small print: Philadelphia's Trea Turner fouled a ball off his right knee Saturday and departed; Boston's Masataka Yoshida left with hamstring tightness; Milwaukee's Brice Turang awaits the machine's opinion of his aching knee.

THE ALMANAC AND DEALINGS DESK: A SHORTSTOP FOR CASH, A NATIONAL AUDIENCE, AND SIX WEEKS TO SETTLE IT ALL

Three entries. First, commerce: the Athletics have sold the shortstop Jonathan Ornelas to Milwaukee for plain cash, and so swift was the conveyance that the man appeared in Brewers flannels that very evening — and was charged with an error for his trouble. Second, spectacle: this afternoon's rubber match between the Cardinals and Cubs goes out to the whole nation upon ABC at a quarter past three Eastern, where young Báez will attempt an encore; the wires observe that no man has ever struck more than three home runs across his first two career games, a record now within a single afternoon's reach. Third, the hourglass: the almanac fixes the final day of the regular season at the twenty-seventh of September — six weeks hence, with every wild-card seat still warm.

The Rest of the Card

MCADOO RATTLES THE WALL AND THE TORONTOS KEEP CLIMBING: CANADIANS 4, HIGHLANDERS 1

With Guerrero consigned to the injured list that very morning, his understudy Charles McAdoo supplied the afternoon's decisive blow — a seventh-inning double off the center-field wall at a hundred and seven miles per hour, inches shy of leaving the premises, scoring the go-ahead run — and added an insurance single in the eighth for good measure. 'It really got the offense going,' the young man said, with some understatement. The Yankee starter Cam Schlittler was hard luck itself, one run across five and a third with seven strikeouts, his league-best earned-run figure settling at 2.19; the New York attack managed four hits, Lombard Jr. driving in the only run. Varland struck out three in the ninth for his eight-and-twentieth save. Toronto has won seven of nine and sits half a game from the American's final wild-card chair; the Bronx men have dropped three running.

TEN INNINGS AT THE TROP, AND THE BALTIMORES TAKE ANOTHER FROM THE LEAGUE'S BEST: O'S 4, GULF COAST CLUB 3

For the second consecutive evening Baltimore inconvenienced the American's finest club. Alonso struck his seven-and-twentieth homer and Encarnacion-Strand his fifth, and the visitors carried a lead into the ninth — whereupon Tampa Bay drew level against Kittredge, the fourth save to spill from his hands this season. The tenth restored order: the deciding run crossed against Baker, and Sanders recorded his third save with the tying man aboard. Seymour struck out nine Orioles in six innings and departed unrewarded. The Rays, at four-and-seventy wins, remain the class of the league but have now dropped two straight; Baltimore, winners of two running, sits half a game from the final wild-card chair.

GRAY THROWS SEVEN BLANK FRAMES FOR HIS CAREER-BEST FIFTEENTH: FENWAY MEN 4, CORSAIRS 0

Sonny Gray, six-and-thirty years of age and pitching like the ace Boston lost when Crochet's shoulder failed, scattered six Pittsburgh hits across seven scoreless innings — working for the first time with the newly arrived Rutschman behind the plate — and collected the fifteenth victory of his season, the most of any campaign in his long career. 'We needed length bad. He gave us length,' said the interim skipper Chad Tracy. Abreu supplied the margin with his two-and-twentieth homer and two doubles besides, and the Fenway men added three in the ninth against Weaver to make the arithmetic comfortable. Boston thus arrests a one-and-six skid; the Corsairs, held to six hits by Gray and company, learn they must also do without Skenes this day, as the infirmary column relates.

THE PALE HOSE TAKE THE SECOND FROM DETROIT AND STRETCH THE GAP TO FOUR AND A HALF: WHITE SOX 4, BENGALS 3

Chicago's grip upon the American's Central tightened another half-turn. C. Montgomery drove in two and Benintendi another, twelve hits in all, while the bullpen — Hicks, Taylor, and Hudson, the last for his fifth save — permitted Detroit a single hit over the final three and two-thirds innings after Kay labored through five and a third. Valencia's sixth homer accounted for two Tiger runs and Torres rapped three hits in the losing cause. 'We play 162. Wherever we end up, we end up,' offered Benintendi, the philosopher of a club that has now won two-and-twenty of five-and-thirty against its own division. Detroit, half a game from the final wild-card chair, has dropped the first two of this heavyweight set.

FOUR IN THE EIGHTH AND THE FISH SWIM PAST CINCINNATI: MARLINS 8, REDLEGS 4

The Queen City men led by a run through seven, whereupon the eighth inning fell upon Antone like a wave: four Miami runs, three of them in a third of an inning, the save spilled and the game reversed. Hernández drove in three for the visitors, Marsee and Mack cleared the wall, and fourteen hits were distributed among the Miami order. For Cincinnati, McLain homered, doubled, and stole a base, and Stewart drove in two to draw level with Abrams atop the National's run-batted-in table at one-and-ninety. The Fish thus even the series and stand three games from the final wild-card chair; the Redlegs have surrendered what the getaway day may yet restore.

SEVEN RUNS WITH TWO OUT IN THE FIFTH, AND BOHM RAPS FIVE: QUAKERS 9, NORTH STARS 1

Alec Bohm went five-for-five with three doubles — the first five-hit evening of his life — and Stott detonated the decisive three-run homer in a fifth inning wherein all seven Philadelphia runs crossed with two men down. The Minnesota starter Prielipp walked three straight at the frame's center, including Arraez — the National's leading batsman at .316 — with the sacks full, and Bohm's single through the middle opened the floodgates. Luzardo struck out nine across six and two-thirds for his eleventh victory. The lone shadow upon the evening was Turner's knee, as the infirmary column relates; the Quakers, at six-and-sixty wins, sit in the three-way knot atop the National's wild-card table.

ONE HIT FOR THE FRIARS AS CLEVELAND CLAIMS ITS MILESTONE: LAKE ERIE MEN 6, PADRES 1

The ten-thousandth victory, saluted in the news columns above, was earned in the old Cleveland style. Cantillo permitted San Diego a single hit across six innings, the visitors' lone run scoring upon a double-play ball in the first, and the relief corps allowed no baserunner thereafter. Kwan and Bailey doubled home runs, the convalescing Ramírez doubled, scored, and added a sacrifice fly, and the seventh brought a double-steal of such larcenous chaos that Cronenworth was charged with two errors upon a single play, DeLauter scampering home behind Kwan. 'That felt kind of reminiscent of old Guards Ball,' Kwan grinned. San Diego's six-game winning streak dies at the lakeshore; the Friars remain knotted with Arizona and Philadelphia for the National's two remaining wild-card chairs.

SINGLES, OF ALL THINGS, CARRY THE DAY IN HOUSTON: PUGET SOUND MEN 10, 'STROS 5

A club that has lived and died by the home run — very nearly half of Seattle's season's runs have arrived via the fence, the largest share in the game — assembled fifteen hits of the humbler variety and administered a thorough beating to the West's leaders, one night after losing to them in the cruelest fashion imaginable. Donovan, restored to the leadoff post, singled home three runs; Young drove in four, capping the evening with his fifteenth homer; Robles tripled amid a four-run second whose punctuation was Young sliding home clean between Naylor's legs. Hancock gave seven sturdy innings. Seattle has now beaten Houston eight times in ten meetings this season and sits five back in the West; the Astros' division lead over Texas is down to two games.

ARENADO STRIKES TWICE AND THE DESERT NINE CLAIM THE SERIES AT ATLANTA: D-BACKS 10, TOMAHAWK NINE 3

Nolan Arenado homered twice — his nineteenth and twentieth — and drove in four, Vargas added a homer and three runs batted in, and Eduardo Rodriguez delivered six innings of two-run ball for his twelfth victory as Arizona seized the series from the East's leaders, Atlanta's fourth home series lost this season. The Atlanta reply amounted to Acuña Jr.'s thirteenth homer and precious little else. 'Everybody in that room believes we can tell a really good story, and our journey is very incomplete,' declared the skipper Torey Lovullo, whose club has won two running, taken series from the Dodgers and now the Braves this month, and sits in the three-way tie for the National's last two wild-card chairs.

MISIOROWSKI KEEPS HIS PROMISE AND THE SUDS MEN STRETCH THE LEAD TO TWO: BREWERS 4, ANGELENOS 1

The young man who vowed to throw the great Ohtani a heater and wish him luck was as good as his word and better: Jacob Misiorowski held Los Angeles to a single run across six innings, his earned-run figure settling at a majestic 1.75 with two hundred and ten strikeouts, both figures the National's finest. Contreras and Ortiz supplied the homers, and Ashby — a starter by trade — closed the final two innings for the first save of his season. The Dodger run was manufactured by the benched-no-more brigade: Call singled and came round upon Ohtani's triple. Milwaukee's lead over Los Angeles for the National's best ledger now stands at two full games, with the rubber match this very afternoon — the bill of fare is posted in the desk note below.

DOWN TO THEIR LAST THREE OUTS, THE AMAZINS STRIKE TWICE: METS 5, CAPITAL NINE 4

Washington carried a one-run lead into the ninth at Flushing, whereupon Cruz was set upon for three hits, two runs crossed, and the Metropolitans walked off winners of two straight. Benge's fourteenth homer and Young's two runs batted in had kept the hosts within reach of House, who drove in three of the Washington runs and homered besides. The victory fell to the animated left-hander Jefry Yan, who furnished the evening's comedy in the top of the frame: he leapt into his celebrated strikeout dance a moment before the umpire declined the call, challenged the verdict, lost it, then struck out Nuñez in earnest moments later and danced a second time, unrepentant. 'I didn't want to look bad, so I had to lock back in,' he explained. The Mets have won seven of ten; the Senators go home lamenting the ninth.

THE LONE STAR NINE CLIMB OUT OF AN EARLY HOLE AND INTO THE FINAL CHAIR: RANGERS 5, MACKMEN 3

Bolte's sixth homer, a three-run affair in the second, staked the Athletics to the early advantage, but Texas answered with patience: a run in the fifth, three in the sixth, and a ninth-inning tally for insurance, Langford's fourteenth homer and two runs batted in leading the charge. Gore ground through five and two-thirds for the victory, Junis — activated from the injured list that very day — bridged an inning without incident, and Latz closed the final two frames for his four-and-twentieth save. The victory snaps a four-game Texas skid and, by the morning's arithmetic, leaves the Rangers in possession of the American's final wild-card chair at two games below the break-even line — with five clubs within a single game of their seat.

DETMERS STRIKES OUT ELEVEN AND WASTES NOT A PITCH OF IT: HALOS 1, ROYALS 0

The finest pitching of the day belonged to Anaheim, where Reid Detmers carried a whitewash through eight innings upon two hits, eleven strikeouts, and not a solitary walk, running his season's count to a hundred and seven-and-sixty, fourth in the American. His opposite Dobnak matched zeroes into the sixth, and the game's only run waited upon the eighth: Frazier doubled and Schanuel drove him home. Joyce closed the ninth with two strikeouts for the save. Kansas City's whole offense amounted to two singles and a stolen base; the Halos have won six of ten, which in the season's basement passes for a heater.

SIX IN THE FOURTH AND WEBB WALKS NO ONE: ORANGE AND BLACK 7, MILE HIGH NINE 1

The Bay men avenged Friday's indignity emphatically. Gilbert struck his sixth homer and drove in three runs, the fourth inning yielded six San Francisco tallies in all, Devers doubled — his nine-and-twentieth two-bagger — and drove in another, and Logan Webb did the professional's work: six innings, four hits, one run, seven strikeouts, and not a walk issued. Lorenzen absorbed his eleventh defeat, and Colorado's brief winning streak perishes at three. The two westernmost cellars conclude their series this afternoon, with the draft arithmetic — the connoisseur's pennant race — hanging in the balance.

The arithmetic desk begs the reader's particular attention this morning, for the American's final wild-card chair has become the most contested furniture in baseball: Texas holds it at one-and-sixty wins against three-and-sixty defeats — two games below the waterline — with Toronto, Baltimore, and Detroit each half a game astern, Minnesota and Cleveland a single game back, and Seattle three. Six claimants within a game of the seat, and not one of them above .500. This day's card runs to fifteen engagements, and two command the front row: at Wrigley Field, a quarter past three Eastern and broadcast to the whole nation upon ABC, young Báez seeks his encore in the rubber match, Dobbins opposite Cabrera; and at Dodger Stadium at ten past four, the National's two finest ledgers settle their series, Henderson and his 2.88 for Milwaukee against Skubal and his 2.93 for Los Angeles, the gap between the clubs standing at two games. The early shift offers Weathers against Cease — he of the 2.40, second-best in the American — at Toronto at 1:37, wherein the Canadians may climb further still. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWICE DOWN TO THE FINAL STRIKE, HOUSTON RISES FIVE RUNS AT A BLOW: WALKER'S WALK-OFF THUNDERBOLT IN THE TENTH — ASTROS 10, MARINERS 7
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 38 · Saturday, the Fifteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 14 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWICE DOWN TO THE FINAL STRIKE, HOUSTON RISES FIVE RUNS AT A BLOW: WALKER'S WALK-OFF THUNDERBOLT IN THE TENTH — ASTROS 10, MARINERS 7

Seattle scores twice in the tenth to seize the lead, whereupon the Houston nine — twice a single strike from defeat against the estimable Muñoz — answers with five runs in the bottom of the frame, Paredes and Varsho supplying the levelers and Christian Walker the three-run blow that empties the dugout, fires the rockets, and stretches the West lead to a season-high three games

Let the reader be advised that the tenth inning at Daikin Park produced seven runs, two lead changes, and one baseball struck so emphatically by Christian Walker that the outcome was never in doubt from the crack of it. The mariners of the Sound had done everything demanded of a visiting club: two runs in the first upon Canzone's single and Naylor's sacrifice fly, a patient recovery after Houston batted round its early deficit, single runs in the sixth and a pair in the eighth to draw level at five, and then two more in the tenth — Robles tripling home one and Rodden lofting home another — to stand three outs from a virtuous road victory with Andrés Muñoz, among the finest closers in the game, upon the hill.

What followed will be recounted in Houston for some while. Twice the count reached its final strike; twice the Astros declined the invitation. Paredes singled home a run — his third driven in of the night — and Varsho singled home the leveler, and then Walker, granted a pitch to his liking, dispatched his three-and-twentieth home run of the season far into the left-field seats with two aboard. Ten runs to seven; fireworks overhead; the entire dugout emptied at the plate. 'To be able to tie it and then force more baseball, and then obviously take the lead, is great,' Walker submitted afterward, with the becoming modesty of a man who has just detonated a ballgame. The earlier chapters ought not be forgotten: Yordan Alvarez opened Houston's account with his six-and-thirtieth home run, the American League's largest crop and a single blow shy of Schwarber's major-league lead, before the hosts stacked four more in the second upon Cam Smith's triple and singles by Peña and Paredes.

The ledger renders the drama consequential: Houston, at three-and-sixty wins, extends its hold upon the American's West to three full games — its most comfortable of the season — over an Arlington club that has now dropped four straight, while Seattle departs six games adrift with but two victories in its last ten. The decision fell to De Los Santos; the defeat, and a seventh spilled save, to the unfortunate Muñoz.

News Around the League

THE MAPLE LEAF NINE HOLD THEIR BREATH: GUERRERO IN THE CONCUSSION PROTOCOL

The gravest bulletin of the evening issued from Toronto, where Vladimir Guerrero Jr. was removed from the Jays' conquest of New York after a chaotic passage at third base in the sixth inning. Racing from first upon an errant throw, Guerrero collided with the Yankee shortstop George Lombard Jr. — the young man's knee meeting the left side of Guerrero's face — and though he rose and completed his journey home with the tying run, he departed the game soon after and now undergoes the full concussion examination. 'You've always got to be careful,' said skipper John Schneider, a man acquainted with such injuries from his own catching days. 'We'll see how he wakes up tomorrow.' The timing is cruel: the Jays have lately been the hottest article in the American's wild-card scrum, and stand now but a single game from the final chair with eight-and-thirty to play. The whole of Ontario awaits the morning's report.

A FIRST SAVE AT ONE HUNDRED MILES AN HOUR, AND THE FRIARS MAKE IT SIX RUNNING

The night's warmest small story belongs to Bradgley Rodriguez, two-and-twenty years of age, who was handed the ninth inning of the Friars' engagement at Cleveland and converted it into the first save of his major-league life — surrendering a leadoff double, then retiring the side with two strikeouts, the last upon a called heater registered at one hundred and eight-tenths miles per hour, the swiftest pitch of the game. 'I'm just very emotional about getting that first save,' the young man confessed. 'The first of many, hopefully.' The established closer Mason Miller, who shares the National's lead at thirty saves, pronounced his understudy 'one of the best relievers in baseball' and professed himself excited in the present tense. The victory, chronicled upon the card below, was San Diego's sixth in succession.

FOUR-AND-THIRTY HOMERS IN MEMPHIS, AND NOW THE BARREL COMES TO THE SHOW

The Mound City club has summoned its No. 3 prospect, the outfielder Joshua Báez, who is expected to make his major-league debut this very day at Wrigley Field. The credentials are considerable: four-and-thirty home runs for Memphis, the largest total in all of Triple-A this season, alongside a .573 slugging figure across one hundred and three games. The wires rank him the nine-and-fiftieth prospect in the game, and St. Louis — whose attack has lately produced three hits in an afternoon, as the card below attests — will not be reviewed harshly for hastening the experiment.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: OHTANI ASCENDS A MOUND, MARTE DESCENDS TO THE TRAINER'S TABLE

The most encouraging admission first: Shohei Ohtani threw four-and-thirty pitches from a bullpen mound before the evening's engagement at Dodger Stadium — his first such session since the July setback that halted his throwing — and employed his full assortment. The stated plan calls for another session or two, then live hitters at least twice, before he pitches in a game; the management contemplates deploying him as a multi-inning opener once he returns. The catchers Will Smith and Dalton Rushing likewise took batting practice upon the field for the first time since their injuries. The debit column: Arizona's Ketel Marte departed the victory at Atlanta in the second inning with soreness of the left knee — an ailment he has been gutting out for some days — and is listed day to day. The Snakes will hold their breath; the man's importance to their wild-card position wants no elaboration.

THE ALMANAC DESK: THE CORN WILL PART AGAIN, AND THE MIDSUMMER CLASSIC GOES TO THE BAY

Three entries for the long calendar. First: scarcely had the Dyersville corn swallowed its last baseball when the league announced the pageant shall return — the Royals and the Red Sox will contest the next MLB at Field of Dreams game on the twelfth of August, 2027. Second: the Giants have been awarded the All-Star Game of 2028, returning the Midsummer Classic to San Francisco for the fourth time and the first since 2007; the 2027 edition remains bound for Wrigley Field. Third, and nearer at hand: the almanac notes the Little League Classic at Williamsport on the three-and-twentieth of this month, Brewers against Braves, a fixture the Herald commends to any reader who enjoys watching millionaires made bashful by twelve-year-olds.

The Rest of the Card

YAMAMOTO DEALS, DÍAZ ATONES, AND THE GAP IS ONE: BOYS IN BLUE 3, BREW CREW 1

The rematch the Herald commended to its readers repaid the vigil. Yoshinobu Yamamoto, made to labor through eight-and-thirty pitches across the first two innings, reorganized his mind — his own account of it — and finished six innings of one-run ball with nine strikeouts, the Milwaukee reply amounting to a solitary sacrifice fly. Betts singled home the game's first run, and Pages and Edman supplied solo homers, the former's twentieth. Then came the ninth and Edwin Díaz, the day after the management renewed its faith in him: two walks, a strikeout, and — at last — three outs, his seventh save and his first since the recent spillage. 'At the end of the day, I made my pitches,' said the closer, plainly relieved. Los Angeles stands one game behind Milwaukee for the National's finest ledger, and the clubs meet again this day.

BURNS RETURNS TO HIS ROOTS AND LOCKS THE DOOR: QUEEN CITY NINE 1, FLORIDIANS 0

The pitching bill the desk praised in advance delivered in full. Young Chase Burns, chastened by his roughest outing a week prior, permitted Miami four singles across seven scoreless innings, striking out eight without a walk — 'just getting back to my roots,' he explained, 'throw it down the middle and let it eat.' His opponent Sandy Alcantara matched him frame for frame, three hits and one run across seven, the run arriving upon Eugenio Suárez's double in the sixth. Burke struck out the side in the eighth and Pagán closed for his fifteenth save. Burns stands four-and-ten against two with an earned-run figure of 2.47, third in the National, and Cincinnati has won two running.

HENDERSON RAPS FOUR AND THE STREAK DIES AT NINE: BIRDS 6, SUNSHINE NINE 5

Gunnar Henderson, whose season has been a long argument with his own reflection, went four-for-four at Tropicana Field — two singles, a double, and a two-run homer in the eighth, his twentieth — and Baltimore snapped Tampa Bay's winning streak at nine. Cowser added his tenth homer and Beavers a two-run single. The hosts made a proper fright of the ninth, three runs arriving upon Aranda's two-run single and Caminero's groundout, before Sanders recorded the final out with the tying run aboard. The Rays remain the American's class at four-and-seventy wins; Henderson, by his own telling, is simply playing 'with my hair on fire' again, and the Birds sit a single game from the final wild-card chair.

HOLMES IS PERFECT THROUGH SIXTEEN MEN IN HIS WRIGLEY UNVEILING: BRUINS 3, REDBIRDS 0

Clay Holmes, lately of both New York establishments, introduced himself to the Wrigley faithful by retiring the first sixteen St. Louis batters in order, the sinker boring holes in the afternoon until Fermín's soft single in the sixth dissolved the dream of history. He settled for six and two-thirds innings of one-hit ball, whereupon Seiya Suzuki supplied the entire offense with a three-run blast, his one-and-twentieth. Webb sealed the whitewash for his ninth save. The Bruins have won eight of ten, sit three behind Milwaukee in the Central, and hold the National's first wild-card chair by seven full games.

FOUR HOMERS ON THE ROAD, TWO FROM VARGAS: SOUTH SIDERS 9, MOTOR CITY NINE 5

The opening engagement of a week that may decide the American's Central went emphatically to Chicago. Miguel Vargas homered twice — his six-and-twentieth and seven-and-twentieth, drawing him level with his own teammate Murakami, who also cleared the wall — and Peters added a two-run shot, while Braden Montgomery drove in three upon a single and a triple. The evening was unkind to young Jobe, scored upon at last in his return and charged with six runs before the fourth was done; Urquidy, in his White Sox debut, collected the victory in relief. 'We know that this week means a lot for us,' said Vargas, and the ledger agrees: the lead over Detroit stands at three and a half.

COLE IS BETRAYED BY THE LEATHER, AND KIRK COLLECTS THE SPOILS: JAYS 3, PINSTRIPES 1

Gerrit Cole, facing Toronto for the first time in two years, delivered five spotless innings and was undone in the sixth by his own infantry: McMahon's low throw and a second error by García upon the same play let the tying run cross — the play upon which Guerrero was injured, as the news column relates — and Kirk promptly doubled home the lead before homering in the eighth for good measure. Bieber took the decision with six innings of one-run ball and Varland closed for his seven-and-twentieth save. Grisham's sixteenth homer was the whole of the New York account; the Pinstripes have dropped two running and remain six and a half behind the Rays.

LINDOR STIRS THE SLEEPING METROPOLITANS: METS 4, SENATORS 1

Washington led at Flushing upon House's single through the middle innings until Francisco Lindor, in the sixth, deposited his twelfth homer and woke the premises. Benge singled home the lead, and Young's eighth homer and Bichette's single fattened it in the seventh. Pintaro collected the first victory of his major-league life with two clean innings of relief, and Senga closed for his second save. The Metropolitans, whatever their station in the ledger, have won seven of ten; the Senators have surrendered the season's series.

PFAADT REPEATS HIMSELF, SEVEN BLANK FRAMES AND ALL: SNAKES 2, ATLANTAS 0

For the second consecutive outing Brandon Pfaadt delivered precisely seven scoreless innings upon two hits — this time with seven strikeouts and not a walk — and for the second consecutive outing his ledger brightened, now seven victories against a single defeat. His opposite Chris Sale struck out nine across six innings of one-run ball and was beaten regardless, the run scoring upon Moreno's groundout in the first; Tawa added a ninth-inning homer for insurance. Garcia closed for his fourth save. Arizona thus claims the opener at Atlanta and holds its wild-card seat, though the club departed the park anxious over Marte's knee, as the infirmary column relates.

THE BUCCANEERS BATTER THE CRIMSON HOSE: BUCS 8, BOSTONS 4

Pittsburgh built its victory upon the long ball and the timely double: Rafael Flores Jr. opened the account with his fourth homer and later singled home another, Valdez doubled home two, and Brandon Lowe's three-run blast in the fifth — his six-and-twentieth — settled the argument at seven-two. Young Chandler took the decision with five innings of two-run ball, and Montgomery recorded the final out for his fourth save after the Bostons crept within four. Duran scored twice in the losing cause. The Bucs have won two running; Boston, at five-and-sixty wins, keeps the second wild-card chair but has dropped six of ten.

CAMPUSANO DOUBLES TWICE AND THE FRIARS' STREAK REACHES SIX: MISSION NINE 7, FOREST CITY NINE 5

Cleveland struck first and often — Nathaniel Lowe homering and singling home another, Rocchio clearing the wall — but the Friars answered with five unanswered upon Bogaerts' two-run homer, Tatis' thirteenth, and Campusano's two-run double, the catcher adding a second double and Bogaerts a sacrifice fly in the seventh. King ground through six innings for the victory over Williams, and the rookie Rodriguez closed matters, as the news column celebrates. San Diego, winners of six straight, stand eight behind Los Angeles in the West but hold the National's second wild-card chair; the Cleveland nine have lost eight of ten.

CAGLIANONE DRIVES IN FIVE AND TROUT IS CUT DOWN AT THE PLATE: ROYAL BLUES 7, SERAPHS 6

A proper slugging match in Anaheim. Jac Caglianone drove in five runs by three separate instruments — a two-run single, a two-run homer, his two-and-twentieth, and the seventh-inning single that drew Kansas City level — and Massey, who had opened the scoring with a homer, singled home the decisive run moments later. The Seraphs' case was argued by Schanuel, whose bases-clearing double and later single produced four runs, and Josh Lowe, whose ninth homer briefly restored the lead; it was undone in part by Rave's right arm, which cut down Mike Trout at the plate upon the tying single in the fifth. Cruz closed for his fourth save.

MCNEIL FALLS A TRIPLE SHY OF THE CYCLE AS THE ELEPHANTS PLAY SPOILER: WHITE ELEPHANTS 8, TEXAS NINE 3

The Athletics, whose remaining schedule is thick with contending neighbors, have announced their intention to make mischief, and Jeff McNeil led the mischief-making: a double, a single, a solo homer, and in the ninth a two-run drive down the right-field line that hopped into the seats — a double when he wanted a triple, leaving the cycle a base short. Cortes had opened matters with a bases-clearing double against the wild Rocker, and after Burger's three-run homer drew Texas level, Butler and the deep men restored order. The defeat, Texas's fourth running, drops the Arlington men three behind Houston and half a game from the final wild-card chair.

FREELAND THROWS EIGHT AND THE MOUNTAIN MEN MAKE IT THREE: ROCKIES 5, JINTS 2

In the season's late-summer curiosities division: Colorado has won three running, the latest upon Kyle Freeland's eight innings of four-hit, one-run craftsmanship by the Bay. Johnston tripled home the first run, Veen cleared the wall with a man aboard, and the Jints' reply was confined to Eldridge's thirteenth homer and Devers' ninth-inning double, his eight-and-twentieth two-bagger of the year. Roupp absorbed his twelfth defeat. The two westernmost clubs in the National's cellar meet again this afternoon, bragging rights and draft arithmetic both in play.

The arithmetic desk directs the reader's attention to the American's final wild-card chair, presently occupied by Detroit at three score wins — with the Twins and Rangers half a game behind, the Jays and Birds a full game, and the Cleveland nine a game and a half: six claimants within a game and a half of one seat, and six weeks to sort them. Tonight's card runs to fifteen engagements, and the bill of fare is rich: at Dodger Stadium, a quarter past seven Eastern, the Brewers hand the ball to Misiorowski — proprietor of the major leagues' finest earned-run figure at 1.76 and two hundred four strikeouts besides — opposite Wrobleski, with the National's best record separated by a single game; the young man's stated plan for the great Ohtani is quoted upon the wires in full: 'I'm going to throw a heater. Good luck. Here it is.' Elsewhere, Schlittler and his American-best 2.21 takes the hill at Toronto at seven minutes past three, and Gray, the American's lone fourteen-game winner, pitches for Boston at Pittsburgh. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: MUNCY MAKES HISTORY, AND MILWAUKEE MAKES OFF WITH THE EVENING: THREE SINGLES IN THE NINTH FELL LOS ANGELES — BREWERS 5, DODGERS 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 37 · Friday, the Fourteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 9 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

MUNCY MAKES HISTORY, AND MILWAUKEE MAKES OFF WITH THE EVENING: THREE SINGLES IN THE NINTH FELL LOS ANGELES — BREWERS 5, DODGERS 4

Max Muncy passes Eric Karros for the most home runs ever struck at Dodger Stadium — with Karros himself at the microphone to call it — and for two innings the Ravine toasts its new record-holder; whereupon Chourio, Mitchell, and Bauers rap three straight singles off the unfortunate Díaz, Megill bars the door, and the Cream City nine departs with its five-and-seventieth victory and the National's finest ledger intact

The evening had written itself a page of history by the sixth inning, and the ninth tore it out and wrote a better one. The historic entry belonged to Max Muncy, summoned from the bench with two aboard and his club trailing by a run: he lifted his three-and-twentieth home run of the season into the right-center seats, and with it passed Eric Karros for the most home runs ever struck at Dodger Stadium — while Karros himself, seated at the broadcast microphone, described the surpassing of his own monument. The blow turned a two-one deficit into a four-two lead and seemed to settle an evening in which Sasaki had wobbled through six innings of two-run ball, the visitors' only scores having arrived by the humblest post: consecutive bases-loaded walks to Ortiz and Hamilton in the fourth.

Then came the ninth, and Edwin Díaz, and the sound of six-and-forty thousand souls falling silent by degrees. Jackson Chourio singled home Ortiz. Garrett Mitchell singled home Hamilton. Jake Bauers singled home Chourio. Three singles, three runs, and every one of the three struck to right field, where Kyle Tucker collected each in turn and could do nothing with any of them. It was the third save Díaz has spilled in his last four chances — a subject upon which the Ravine's management pronounced itself this morning, as the news column relates — and it handed the decision to Hall, who had faced six Los Angeles batters across the seventh and eighth and retired every one, three by strikeout. Megill closed the ninth without incident for his two-and-twentieth save.

The ledger stands thus: five-and-seventy wins against seven-and-forty for the Cream City nine, the National League's finest account, four games clear of the North Siders in the Central — while Los Angeles, at three-and-seventy and nine-and-forty, let slip its chance to draw level with the leaders and must content itself with an eight-game cushion over San Diego in the West. The same two clubs resume hostilities tonight at ten past ten Eastern, Gasser opposing Yamamoto, and the Herald recommends the reader lose no sleep deciding whether to stay up: the answer is yes.

News Around the League

THE CORN PARTS, AND SIX-AND-TWENTY IMMORTALS WALK OUT OF IT

Dyersville, Iowa, got its pageant at last, and the pageant did not disappoint. Before the third MLB at Field of Dreams game, six-and-twenty members of the Hall of Fame emerged from the outfield corn precisely as the ghost players did in the famous moving picture, a procession to raise the hackles on the flintiest scorer's neck. The game that followed belonged to Philadelphia — the score and particulars are set down upon the card below — and above all to Kyle Schwarber, who deposited two baseballs into that same corn, his six-and-thirtieth and seven-and-thirtieth of the campaign, the largest crop in the major leagues. 'Is this heaven?' the Philadelphia wires asked afterward, and answered themselves in the affirmative. The beaten Minnesotans were gracious in their turn, pronouncing the evening one they would cherish for a lifetime — which is, the Herald submits, the entire point of building a ballpark in a cornfield.

DEGROM DEPARTS AFTER TWO, AND ARLINGTON HOLDS ITS BREATH

The gravest news of the evening came from Anaheim, where Jacob deGrom left his start against the Angels after but two innings, the club citing fatigue of the right triceps. The Lone Star staff has absorbed one blow after another this season, and the timing of this one could scarcely be worse: the Rangers have now dropped three straight, sit two games behind Houston in the American's West, and cling to the wild-card scrum by half a game. Such comfort as exists arrives by rehabilitation wire — Jack Leiter has been dispatched to Round Rock to begin working his way back.

THREE THOUSAND INNINGS FOR THE OLD LION

Let the milestone desk record that Max Scherzer, laboring in Toronto flannels against Boston last evening, crossed the threshold of three thousand career innings pitched — only the second active practitioner to reach that figure. The evening's decision went against him, as the card below relates, but five innings of one-run ball from an arm with three thousand frames upon its odometer is its own kind of testimony. The Herald tips its cap to endurance itself.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: TWO ELBOWS, A KNEE, AND SOME BRIGHTER BULLETINS

The overnight admissions: Boston has placed Garrett Whitlock on the fifteen-day list with inflammation of the right elbow; Detroit has lost James Outman to the seven-day concussion list; and Pittsburgh's Endy Rodríguez goes down with an ailing hip. In Milwaukee the ranking worry is Brice Turang, who sat out the Dodger engagement with a balky knee while the club seeks a second reading of his examination. The brighter bulletins: Byron Buxton was activated in time to patrol the Dyersville corn and doubled for good measure; Carlos Rodón struck out seven in a rehabilitation outing and stands on the verge of rejoining the New York rotation; and Shohei Ohtani has progressed to long toss, with work off a mound reported the next station on his return to pitching.

WIRES FROM THE RAVINE: THE CLOSER KEEPS HIS OFFICE

Two dispatches from Los Angeles beyond the evening's defeat. First, the management declared this morning that Edwin Díaz, his three spilled saves in four chances notwithstanding, remains the club's closer — skipper Dave Roberts professing his faith undiminished. Second, on the matter of the club's possible sale: a source tells the Eastern wire that Ohtani would likely decline to exercise the so-called key-man clause in his contract — the escape hatch permitting him to opt out should Mark Walter sell the franchise. The deed to the ballclub may change hands or may not; the great man's services, it appears, are not going anywhere either way.

The Rest of the Card

SCHWARBOMBS AMONG THE CORNSTALKS: PHILS 7, MINNESOTANS 1

The particulars of the Dyersville festival, pageantry aside: Schwarber opened the scoring with a solo blast in the first and added a two-run shot in the fourth — numbers six-and-thirty and seven-and-thirty, both swallowed by the corn — while Nola dealt five innings of one-run ball with nine strikeouts for the victory. Marsh added a two-run homer, his seventeenth, and Harper and Stott singled home a run apiece. Young Keaschall's solo shot was the whole of the Minnesota reply, charged ultimately to Bradley, who fell to nine-and-five. The Phils, at five-and-sixty wins, keep their grip on the National's final wild-card chair.

STEWART IS STRUCK, THE BENCHES EMPTY, AND CINCINNATI HAS THE FINAL WORD: REDLEGS 9, PALE HOSE 8

A rough evening on the South Side by every measure. The Redlegs struck three times in the first — Sal Stewart's six-and-twentieth homer followed by Suárez's two-run blow — and tempers followed the baseballs out of the yard: Davis Martin was ejected after striking Stewart with a pitch, the benches emptying for their airing. Chicago twice clawed level or ahead behind Grichuk's pair of doubles, but Stephenson's three-run homer in the fourth restored Cincinnati's command at eight-four, and Suárez — four runs driven in, one of them forced home by a bases-full plunking — kept the hosts at arm's length. Chicago crept within a single run on Quero's third hit of the night in the ninth before Garcia shut the gate for his second save. The Pale Hose still hold the American's Central by two and a half over Detroit; Stewart's nine-and-eightieth run driven in stands second in the National.

NOT ONE STRIKEOUT, AND NOT ONE RUN EITHER: BENGALS 3, LAKE ERIE MEN 0

The Detroit pitchers — Montero across six and a third, Holton in relief, Jansen for the fifteenth save — achieved a whitewash without recording a solitary strikeout, a feat the wires pronounce among the rarest in the pitching art. The runs arrived modestly: a groundout by Dingler, a solo homer by Valencia, a single by Torkelson. Messick deserved better than his defeat, five and two-thirds innings of two-run ball leaving his 2.59 mark third among the American's pitchers. The Bengals sit two and a half behind the Pale Hose and hold the league's final wild-card chair.

ASHCRAFT GOES THE FULL ROUTE AND THE CORSAIRS RUN RIOT: CORSAIRS 13, FISH 1

Braxton Ashcraft delivered the completest of complete games — nine innings, three hits, ten strikeouts — for his twelfth victory, and his confederates buried Miami beneath sixteen hits. Triolo homered (the reviewing magistrates upheld it), Rafael Flores Jr. cleared the wall twice, and Jacob Gonzalez crowned a five-run ninth with a two-run shot. Caissie's thirteenth homer, in the ninth, spared the Fish the indignity of a blanking. Miami slips to two-and-sixty wins and sits two and a half from the wild-card scrum.

ONE SWING FROM WILSON, SIX INNINGS FROM GILBERT, AND NOT A RUN TO SPARE: M'S 1, BRONX BOMBERS 0

In the Bronx, on the mound he confesses he dreamed of pitching upon, Logan Gilbert dealt six scoreless innings with seven strikeouts, and Weston Wilson's second-inning homer off Fried — his fourth of the year — stood as the game entire. Bazardo, Ferrer, and Muñoz, the last for his one-and-twentieth save, carried the single run home like porcelain. The victory arrests a Seattle slide that had reached six games; New York, for its part, wasted five sturdy innings from Fried and still holds the American's first wild-card chair, six and a half behind the streaking Rays.

TOLLE THROWS EIGHT BLANK FRAMES AND DURBIN CLEARS THE SACKS: HUB NINE 7, TORONTOS 0

Young Payton Tolle permitted Toronto two hits across eight scoreless innings — an evening that drew rave notice even from the opposing manager — and Caleb Durbin supplied the thunder: a grand slam in the eighth, his twelfth homer, and five runs driven in altogether. Contreras opened the scoring with a first-inning double. The defeat went to Scherzer on his three-thousandth-inning night, chronicled in the news column above. Boston's second straight victory since arresting its five-game slide keeps the Hub nine in the second wild-card chair at five-and-sixty wins.

CAVALLI CARRIES A NO-HITTER INTO THE SEVENTH AT WRIGLEY: CAPITAL NINE 7, NORTH SIDERS 0

Cade Cavalli held the North Siders hitless into the seventh inning and finished with a single hit allowed across eight, ten strikeouts, and his tenth victory — the latest and loudest chapter in the young man's ascent. Crews doubled home the first run, and Abimelec Ortiz struck a three-run homer in a five-run fifth that settled matters; Gausman absorbed the defeat, his eleventh. The whitewash trims Chicago's account to four games behind Milwaukee in the Central, though the club still holds the National's first wild-card seat by a comfortable six and a half.

TROUT RAPS THREE AND THE HALOS MAKE IT THREE RUNNING: HALOS 7, LONE STAR NINE 0

Mike Trout, the old lion of Anaheim in full August voice, collected three hits and a run driven in — the wires liken his current stretch to the vintage of 2018 — while Ureña spun six scoreless innings for the victory. Josh Lowe and Siri drove home two apiece as the Halos ran their winning streak to three. The evening's costlier news for Texas was deGrom's early departure, set down in the news column above; the Lone Star nine has now dropped three straight and holds the wild-card cellar door by its fingernails, half a game behind Detroit.

A card of nine produced five whitewashes — the arithmetic desk begs the reader to check it, and it holds: three by the count of seven-nought, one by three, and one by the barest one-nought. Tonight the schedule swells to fourteen engagements, and the desk directs the connoisseur thus: the heavyweight rematch in Los Angeles at ten past ten, Gasser opposing Yamamoto and his 2.65; a pitching bill of rare quality at Cincinnati at ten past six, where Alcantara, thirteen-and-six, meets young Burns, thirteen-and-two; the Rays, riding nine straight, at home to receive Baltimore; and in Detroit, young Jobe — unscored upon in the young life of his return — takes the hill against Newcomb of the Pale Hose. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: ELEVEN YEARS A BIG-LEAGUER, AND NEVER A NIGHT LIKE THIS: BREGMAN STRIKES THREE CIRCUITS, DRIVES IN SEVEN — CUBS 12, SENATORS 6
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 36 · Thursday, the Thirteenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

ELEVEN YEARS A BIG-LEAGUER, AND NEVER A NIGHT LIKE THIS: BREGMAN STRIKES THREE CIRCUITS, DRIVES IN SEVEN — CUBS 12, SENATORS 6

A Monday spent spelunking the video archives yields a Wednesday for the ages, as the Chicago third sacker authors the first three-homer game of his long and decorated life — Swanson adds a circuit and a two-bagger, Suzuki drives home two more, and the Bruins' eighth victory in ten keeps them three behind Milwaukee with a wild-card cushion of luxurious proportions

The affair began not at the ball orchard but in a dim room on Monday, the Cubs' idle day, where Alex Bregman sat burrowed down a rabbit hole of video archives, comparing the swing of this August against swings from every station of his career — some of the footage a full decade old, older than his major-league life itself. Whatever the gentleman found in those flickering frames, he carried it to Washington and applied it without mercy: a three-run blast in the fifth, moments after Crow-Armstrong's tying two-bagger had leveled a one-all knot, then a two-run shot in the sixth, and a third in the eighth — his fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the season, seven runs driven in, both figures the finest of an eleven-year career that had never before contained a three-homer evening.

His confederates were scarcely idle. Dansby Swanson doubled and homered besides — his eighteenth — Seiya Suzuki singled home two, and Crow-Armstrong's double was his four-and-twentieth as the visitors piled up twelve runs. Peterson labored five innings for his seventh victory, and Assad swallowed the final four frames whole for a save of the old-fashioned length. The Senators gave honest resistance — young Lile drove in three, and Ortiz and Tena each cleared the wall — but the unfortunate Cosgrove, charged with three runs while recording but one out, bore the defeat.

The ledger now reads thus: Chicago stands at one-and-seventy wins against fifty defeats, eight victories in its last ten, three games behind Milwaukee in the National's Central — and holding the league's first wild-card chair by a luxurious seven and a half games. When a man eleven years in the trade finds something new in the old films, the Herald observes, the whole division is advised to look to its locks.

News Around the League

NINE UP, NINE DOWN: THE RAYS COMPLETE THE PERFECT VOYAGE

Let the almanac make room, for the Gulf Coast club has done a thing without precedent in its own annals and nearly without precedent anywhere: nine games upon the western seaboard, nine victories, the first unbeaten road trip of such length in the franchise's history — and, the wires attest, only the second time in the whole chronicle of the majors that an East Coast club has swept a West Coast swing of nine. Wednesday's finale in Sacramento, an eight-to-four dismissal of the White Elephants chronicled upon the card below, ran the winning streak to nine straight and the season's account to four-and-seventy wins against six-and-forty defeats — the American's finest ledger, nine and one in the last ten. The connoisseur of omens will note that the Tampa men now fly home to receive Baltimore on the morrow, having misplaced the knack of losing somewhere over the Rockies.

FREEMAN TUMBLES INTO THE ENEMY'S PARLOR, AND RISES SMILING

A gasp went round Chavez Ravine on Wednesday evening when Freddie Freeman, pursuing a foul pop with his customary zeal, went headlong down the steps and into the visitors' dugout — a frightening spill that emptied both benches of their breath. The happy intelligence: the first sacker rose without serious injury, reporting soreness of the shoulder, hand, knee, and foot — 'total body soreness,' by his own cheerful census — and professing himself chiefly glad that his head went unstruck. The champions will take the bruises over the alternative, for the man's bat remains very much required in the pennant arithmetic.

SIX CLUBS OVERTAKEN IN A MONTH: THE PADRES' REMARKABLE ASCENT

The wires pause over a piece of standings archaeology worth the printing: one month ago, the San Diego nine sat buried in the National's wild-card queue with six clubs stacked above them, and their direction at the Trade Deadline was a matter of open debate in their own front office. General manager A.J. Preller chose to buy, and the club has repaid him with interest — five straight victories now, five-and-sixty wins in sum, and as of this morning a wild-card chair held all their own, a full game clear of Arizona and Philadelphia, who must share the bench behind them at level records. Last evening's eleven-inning escape against Milwaukee, set down upon the card below, was the sort of victory that separates the climbers from the climbed-over.

THE YOUTH DESK: A DAUGHTER OF THE BIGS PITCHES ALABAMA TO WILLIAMSPORT

From the junior circuits, a story to warm the flintiest scorer's heart: Kinley Rasmus, daughter of the former big-league pitcher Cory Rasmus, spun a complete-game shutout to send her Phenix City, Alabama nine to the Little League World Series — the town's first such expedition since 1999, seven-and-twenty years in the waiting. The Herald tips its cap to the young lady and notes, for the benefit of posterity, that command of the strike zone would appear to travel in the blood.

THE ALMANAC: THE CORN AWAITS ITS THIRD HARVEST THIS EVENING

Tonight the main attraction arrives at Dyersville: the Twins and the Quakers contest the third MLB at Field of Dreams game, first pitch at half past seven Eastern, carried to the nation by Netflix — the pageant's first staging in four years, the famous diamond in the corn having lately undergone an extensive refurbishment. Philadelphia's Bryson Stott, ever the connoisseur of ceremonial haberdashery, plans custom gear paying homage to Phillies now passed from this world. The prospects christened the same stage Wednesday afternoon, the National League side edging the American in the High School All-American Game. The almanac desk further notes the Little League Classic at Williamsport on the three-and-twentieth, Brewers against Braves, and reminds the record that the regular campaign closes the seven-and-twentieth of September.

The Rest of the Card

ELEVEN INNINGS, ONE WALK-OFF, AND A WILD-CARD CHAIR ALL THEIR OWN: SAN DIEGO NINE 4, MILWAUKEES 3

Twice the visitors poked their noses ahead, and twice the hosts pulled them back by the coattails. Bogaerts answered an early two-nought deficit with his tenth circuit, Cronenworth singled home the equalizer in the eighth, and when Gary Sánchez — who had homered earlier — doubled Milwaukee ahead in the eleventh, San Diego replied in the bottom half: Merrill's sacrifice fly leveled the account, and Campusano lined the winning single to bring Sung-Mun Song dancing home. Morejon pocketed his ninth victory against two defeats; Senzatela, charged in the eleventh with the equalizer and the fatal blow alike, took the loss. Five straight now for the climbers of the news column above; three straight defeats for the Milwaukees, whose Central cushion over the Cubs has thinned to three.

LEWIS DOUBLES TWICE AND THE TWINS OUT-SLUG THE BIRDS: TWIN CITIES NINE 7, ORIOLES 5

Royce Lewis, the centerpiece the wires pronounce restored to his old form at precisely the needful hour, smote two doubles among Minnesota's fourteen hits, and Bell, Caratini, and young Roden — three hits himself — kept the parade moving through a four-run third and a two-run fifth. Baltimore's Beavers had briefly turned the game with a three-run blast in the third, and Taveras homered in the ninth, but Baz was relieved of nine hits and five runs in three innings and fell to four-and-twelve. Matthews took the victory, Gómez the seventeenth save, and the Twin Cities nine crept within half a game of the American's final wild-card chair.

LEAHY BESTS WHEELER HIMSELF, AND THE REDBIRDS TAKE THE SERIES: REDBIRDS 7, QUAKERS 1

The billing read Zack Wheeler, ten-and-three; the evening belonged to Leahy, who dealt five innings of one-run ball with six strikeouts and improved to nine-and-four in a stretch the St. Louis wires call his finest. The hosts pried Wheeler open with four runs in the fifth — Herrera singling, Burleson doubling home two, Walker doubling home another — and Burleson returned in the seventh to finish with three runs driven in, his four-and-eightieth of the season drawing him level with Walker among the National's leaders. Philadelphia managed but Arraez's run-scoring double, dropped the series, and slid into the wild-card tie with Arizona; the Redbirds, winners of seven in their last ten, lurk but two and a half back.

THE PERFECT NINE SEALED IN SACRAMENTO: TAMPA MEN 8, WHITE ELEPHANTS 4

The finale of the immortal road trip (see the leading dispatch of the news column) was settled early: two in the second, one in the third on Mullins' double, and then a four-run fourth crowned by Liam Hicks' three-run circuit, his sixteenth, part of a three-RBI evening. Rasmussen cruised five innings for his twelfth victory while Caminero singled home his seven-and-seventieth run driven in. Gelof and Butler homered late in the Elephant cause, whose Perkins absorbed twelve hits and fell to two-and-nine. Nine straight victories for the Gulf Coast club; eight defeats in ten for the hosts.

VEEN, ONE DAY RECALLED, STRIKES HIS FIRST — AND THE SNAKES SLIP FROM THEIR CHAIR: ROX 6, SNAKES 4

The reader will recall young Zac Veen passing through Tuesday's shuttle desk, recalled from the minors; on Wednesday he introduced himself properly with a two-run circuit, his first of the campaign, to follow a four-run second crowned by Brett Sullivan's three-run blast — all six runs charged to Kelly, who fell to eight-and-ten. Arizona clawed back on Carroll's eighteenth homer and fourteenth triple, but Feltner held the line, Romano notarized the twelfth save, and the Coloradans — the National's rearmost club, and lately a recurring nuisance to this particular opponent — took their second straight from the Desert nine. The defeat is costly: Arizona wakes level with Philadelphia, a game behind San Diego, its wild-card chair now a shared bench.

TWO SACRIFICE FLIES SUFFICE FOR THE SERIES: ASTROS 2, FRISCO NINE 1

The Houston bats spent the afternoon in church, managing no run-scoring hit whatever, and won the series anyway. Down one-nought from the first inning on Bericoto's single, the visitors drew level in the seventh on Velázquez's sacrifice fly and ahead in the eighth on Nick Allen's — the winning run charged to Winn, whose blown save turned into the defeat. Okert took the victory, Hader the seventeenth save, and the Astros fled Oracle Park with the American West's lead preserved at a game and a half over Texas, beaten simultaneously down the coast. The Orange and Black, who parted with one of their best pitchers and their best hitter at the Deadline, gave every ounce they had left.

THE DEADLINE MEN EARN THEIR WAGES AND THE SKID IS SNAPPED: FOREST CITY NINE 6, MOTOR CITY NINE 4

Cleveland's July purchases delivered in a bundle: Griffin labored five innings of one-earned-run ball for his thirteenth victory against four defeats, Jo Adell struck a two-run circuit — his eighteenth — and Nathaniel Lowe stretched to save the ninth-inning throw that helped seal it. Angel Martínez doubled twice, young Genao doubled home a run — his first two-bagger of the campaign — and Smith struck out three across the final four outs for his one-and-thirtieth save, the American's most. Detroit had its moments — Torres homered, Torkelson doubled home two — but Valdez walked five and paid for it. The Forest City nine thus halt a skid that had reached three-and-seven over ten; the Detroits slip to a half-game behind Minnesota in the wild-card queue.

A FOUR-RUN THIRD AND JUNK OF THE FINEST QUALITY: GULF STREAM NINE 8, BUCS 2

Miami batted around to profit in the third — Ramírez doubling home one, Jiménez struck by a pitch with the sacks full, Mack walking home another, Edwards adding a sacrifice fly to his earlier run-scoring single — and Mlodzinski did not survive the frame, charged with four runs in two and a third. Junk, whose surname the headline desk declines to resist, delivered six innings of one-earned-run pitching for the victory, while Conine and Heriberto Hernández added circuits for garnish. Four straight now for the Floridians, two-and-sixty wins and the National's most formidable home ledger, a game and a half shy of the wild-card scrum; the Bucs have dropped three running.

JONES IN THE THREE-HOLE, GRISHAM TWICE OVER THE WALL: PINSTRIPES 10, SEATTLE NINE 5

With Judge and Bellinger both consigned to the sidelines, the management installed towering young Spencer Jones third in the order as a statement of belief, and the lad answered with two doubles and three runs driven in. Seattle had built a four-to-one lead on circuits by Arozarena, Rodríguez, and Canzone, whereupon New York dismantled it piece by piece: Grisham's fourteenth homer, Jones' tying double, a three-run seventh opened by Grisham's go-ahead two-bagger, and Grisham again in the eighth — a two-run circuit, his second of the night, four runs driven in altogether. Blackburn took the win in relief. The Pinstripes hold the American's top wild-card seat at eight-and-sixty wins; the mariners of the Sound have now dropped six straight and sink from view.

FIVE RUNS IN THE EIGHTH AND BOSTON'S SLIDE REACHES FIVE: MAPLE LEAF NINE 6, CRIMSON HOSE 4

For seven innings the game was a taut one-to-one affair, José Soriano — making his first home start in Toronto flannels since his arrival — dealing handsomely, and Contreras's four-and-twentieth homer accounting for the whole Boston offense. Then the eighth: Okamoto singled the go-ahead run home, Clement walked with the bases full, Springer lifted a sacrifice fly, and Straw doubled home two more, all five runs laid at the door of Guerrero, who retired nobody. Boston scored thrice in the ninth before Varland shut the gate for his six-and-twentieth save. Three straight for the Jays; five straight defeats for the Crimson Hose, whose grip on the second wild-card chair loosens by the evening.

MAHLE MAKES THE FRONT OFFICE LOOK PROPHETIC: TOMAHAWK NINE 6, FLUSHING NINE 3

Atlanta declined to purchase a frontline starter at the Deadline, the wires observed at the time, with some tartness; Tyler Mahle, the starter they did purchase, keeps performing like one. Six innings, four hits, a single run, seven strikeouts — never mind the four-and-nine record he carries like borrowed luggage. Thomas, Yastrzemski, and Riley all cleared the wall, Acuña singled home another and doubled besides, and the Braves banked their three-and-seventieth victory. The Flushing nine answered with circuits from Bichette, Robert Jr., and Torrens, and nothing else; Thornton pitched six creditable innings and lost anyway.

CASTILLO STRIKES OUT TEN AND THE SOUTH SIDERS PITCH A WHITEWASH: SOUTH SIDERS 5, QUEEN CITY NINE 0

Luis Castillo, the Deadline acquisition his manager salutes as 'a dog,' showed precisely why the South Siders paid for him: seven innings, one solitary hit, ten strikeouts — a season's best — and not a Cincinnati runner crossed all night. Drew Romo homered and drove in two, Meidroth added a two-run circuit, his twelfth, and Lowder took the defeat despite honest work. The shutout preserves Chicago's grip on the American's Central at three and a half games; the Reds, whitewashed entire, would prefer the whole evening stricken from the record.

OHTANI AND BETTS SUPPLY THE THUNDER, KNACK THE LONG SEAL: BOYS IN BLUE 4, ROYAL BLUES 2

Betts — fourteen the night before, fifteen now — answered Kansas City's first strike with a game-tying circuit, Shohei Ohtani's seven-and-twentieth, a two-run blow in the third, turned the lead for good, and the catcher Feduccia added a solo shot while Lauer dealt six and a third sturdy innings for his seventh victory. Knack recorded the final eight outs for his first save of the year, and the champions completed the sweep of the Royal blues, their third straight win, with the Milwaukees arriving tonight for the collision of the National's two best ledgers. The evening's fright — Freeman's plunge into the visitors' dugout — is chronicled with relief in the news column above.

TROUT COLLECTS THREE AND YOUNG KLASSEN HIS FIRST: SERAPHS 5, ARLINGTON MEN 2

Mike Trout, the old lion of Anaheim, rapped three hits, drove in two, and stole his tenth base, while George Klassen, a pitcher of no previous major-league victories, dealt six innings of five-hit ball to claim his first. Texas led two-to-one behind Seager's twelfth homer until the sixth, when Jose Siri emerged from the bench to double home the equalizer and Ahlstrom was charged with three runs while recording one out — blown save and defeat in a single tidy parcel. Joyce closed the door for his first save of the year. The Arlington men have now dropped two straight and sit a game and a half behind Houston, clinging to the American's final wild-card chair with three clubs breathing within a game of them.

A card of nine this Thursday, and the desk directs the connoisseur's attention as follows: the sentimental centerpiece is at Dyersville, half past seven Eastern, where the Quakers send Nola against Bradley of the Twins in the Field of Dreams game, carried by Netflix to every parlor in the republic. The heavyweight bill is out west at ten past ten, the Milwaukees at the Boys in Blue — four-and-seventy wins against three-and-seventy, the National's two stoutest ledgers colliding under the western lights, with further engagements to follow Friday and Saturday. The early shift offers a rubber match in Detroit at ten past one, Messick and his 2.57 opposing Montero, and the Crimson Hose attempt to arrest their five-game slide in Toronto at 3:07, though the assignment runs through Scherzer, who awaits them. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
