entry.title: SEVENTEEN HITS, ONE GRAND SALVO, AND A LOGJAM AT THE WILD-CARD TABLE: FRIARS 11, BREWERS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 35 · Wednesday, the Twelfth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SEVENTEEN HITS, ONE GRAND SALVO, AND A LOGJAM AT THE WILD-CARD TABLE: FRIARS 11, BREWERS 2

San Diego falls upon the owners of the game's best ledger with five runs before the second inning is old — Rengifo's bases-full blow the cannonade, Campusano three times a tormentor, and Tatis Jr. ascending to second place in the whole history of Friar slugging — whereby three clubs now sit level as a billiard table, contesting two October chairs

The Cream City nine arrived in San Diego owning baseball's handsomest account, four-and-seventy wins against six-and-forty defeats, and were sent to bed having absorbed an eleven-to-two thrashing — their second defeat running, and the Friars' fourth consecutive victory. The decisive business was transacted early: in the second inning Jake Cronenworth doubled home a run, and Luis Rengifo, a gentleman carrying but two home runs on the season's ledger, selected that moment for his third — a grand slam to left field, four runs across on a single swing, and a five-nought advantage before the visitors had rightly settled into their seats.

The procession scarcely slackened thereafter. Fernando Tatis Jr. struck his twelfth circuit in the fourth — a blow of historical freight, for it carried him past every Friar save one and installed him second upon the club's all-time home-run roll, behind only Manny Machado, his teammate still, who marked the occasion with three hits of his own. Luis Campusano went three-for-four with a homer and three runs driven in, Jackson Merrill doubled home another, and by the close the hosts had amassed seventeen hits while Walker Buehler — six innings, one run — pocketed the victory. The unfortunate Harrison, nine-and-three on the year, was charged with eight runs and did not survive the fifth.

The arithmetic is where the evening turns consequential. At four-and-sixty wins against seven-and-fifty defeats, San Diego now stands precisely level with Arizona and Philadelphia — three clubs at .529, crowding two wild-card chairs, with the Cubs comfortably above the scrum. Milwaukee's lead in the National's Central remains a plump four games, but the Friars have now taken consecutive series from first-place opposition, and they play like men who have read the schedule.

News Around the League

THE CROWN OF CIRCUITS: FOUR CLAIMANTS AT FIVE-AND-THIRTY, THE CLOSEST RACE IN FORTY YEARS

The wires devote their lead column to a spectacle not witnessed in four decades: a home-run race packed four deep. Junior Caminero of Tampa Bay and Matt Olson of Atlanta each struck his five-and-thirtieth last evening, drawing level with Houston's Yordan Alvarez — resident at that figure since late July — and Philadelphia's Kyle Schwarber. Four men, five-and-thirty circuits apiece, and Colorado's Hunter Goodman lurking a single blow behind at four-and-thirty. The connoisseur is advised to keep the almanac handy through September; the crown may be decided by a single evening's swing.

THE CATCHER PRIZE UNVEILED: RUTSCHMAN TAKES HIS BOW IN BOSTON FLANNELS

The debut these pages heralded yesterday is now in the books: Adley Rutschman, Boston's great prize of the Trade Deadline, was formally activated and caught his first game in Crimson employ at Toronto, collecting a single hit and drawing two walks in the five-to-three defeat chronicled upon the card below. The reinforcement could scarcely be more wanted — the Hub nine have now dropped four running — and the veteran Jake Rogers was designated for assignment to clear the perch. One debut does not arrest a slide, but Boston's followers will take the omen over the alternative.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: GREENE AND TREINEN CONSIGNED TO THE LONG LIST, TAILLON'S FEARS CONFIRMED

A somber morning's ledger for the medical men. Cincinnati has transferred Hunter Greene to the sixty-day list with soreness of the right elbow, and Los Angeles has done likewise with the reliever Blake Treinen, his complaint an inflammation of the same joint. In Toronto the examiners returned their verdict on Jameson Taillon, whose early exit from his Blue Jays debut these pages reported yesterday: tendinitis of the right forearm, and a fifteen-day sentence. Miami, for its part, has shelved Kyle Stowers with a strained left hamstring.

The brighter beds: Tampa Bay has dispatched Shane McClanahan on a rehabilitation errand to Durham, Pittsburgh has sent Oneil Cruz to Altoona on the same business, and Kansas City's Vinnie Pasquantino is mending at Omaha.

THE SHUTTLE DESK: SUMMONED AT NOON, PRODUCING BY NIGHTFALL

The day's roster traffic repaid its paperwork with unusual promptness. Texas selected Jarred Kelenic from Round Rock, and by evening he had singled home a run in Anaheim; Cincinnati summoned the first baseman Michael Toglia from Louisville, and within hours he stood in the middle of the eighth-inning uprising that turned the Chicago engagement; and Toronto recalled the reliever Chase Lee from Buffalo, who required but a few innings to collect his first victory of the year against Boston. Colorado, tidying its own shelves, recalled the outfielder Zac Veen and designated Edouard Julien for assignment. The express between the high minors and the show, the Herald observes, has seldom run so profitably on time.

THE ALMANAC: THE CORN IS OCCUPIED ALL WEEK AT DYERSVILLE

The Iowa corn has itself a full engagement book. The minor leaguers christened the Field of Dreams stage Tuesday evening — the wires pronounce the occasion properly magical, nostalgia hanging in the air alongside the humidity — and this very afternoon, at two o'clock Eastern, the High School All-American Game takes the same diamond, the first time the prospect showcase has been staged at Dyersville. The main attraction arrives upon the morrow: the Twins and Phillies contest the Field of Dreams game proper on Thursday evening. The regular campaign's final day, the almanac desk reminds the record, remains the twenty-seventh of September.

The Rest of the Card

THE PRODIGY McGONIGLE DRIVES IN THREE AND THE BENGALS KEEP ROARING: BENGALS 6, LAKE ERIE MEN 4

Young Kevin McGonigle, batting at a cool .288, delivered a two-run double in a three-run fifth and singled home another in the seventh, and Detroit collected its third straight victory — eight of its last ten — despite mustering but six hits. Chase DeLauter and Jo Adell homered in the Cleveland cause and Bibee absorbed his twelfth defeat; Jansen sealed the fourteenth save. The Bengals now breathe two and a half games behind the Pale Hose in the American's Central, while the Lake Erie men have dropped eight of ten and are running short of season.

EURY THE MAGNIFICENT OUTDUELS SKENES HIMSELF: FISH 2, CORSAIRS 0

Eury Pérez, who aspires aloud to the game's first rank of pitchers, presented his credentials in the most direct fashion: seven scoreless innings, three hits, seven strikeouts, with Paul Skenes — no small examiner — in the opposite corner. Esteury Ruiz homered in the third — his sixth — then stole his eight-and-twentieth base and came round on Edwards' single for the second tally, and Fairbanks notarized the eighteenth save. The Fish have won three running and sit two games above level water, hunting the wild-card scrum from two and a half back.

THE ONE-TWO PUNCH LANDS AGAIN: NORTH SIDERS 8, CAPITAL NINE 6

Pete Crow-Armstrong struck his seven-and-twentieth circuit and Seiya Suzuki, batting in his shadow, added his twentieth alongside a run-scoring double, while Alex Bregman crossed three times and homered besides. Washington answered gamely — Abrams' nine-and-twentieth brought his league-leading total to one-and-ninety runs driven in, and Crews and Young also cleared the wall — but the arithmetic favored Chicago, eight victories now in its last ten and holding the National's first wild-card chair by a comfortable six and a half games. Rolison improved to seven-and-one; Webb sealed the eighth save.

FOUR IN THE SEVENTH AND THE BOMBERS ESCAPE AGAIN: BRONX BOMBERS 4, PUGET SOUND MEN 1

For six innings the evening belonged to the pitchers, Woo dealing five scoreless for Seattle and Weathers conceding only Arozarena's fifteenth homer. Then came the seventh and the now-customary New York uprising: Ryan McMahon singled home two and Trent Grisham two more, all charged to the unhappy Rucker, and Bednar closed the seven-and-twentieth save. The manner is nerve-wracking, the manager confesses, but it is working — the Bombers hold the American's top wild-card seat at seven-and-sixty wins. Seattle has now lost five straight, and the backstop Raleigh, hitless again with his average sunk to .159, minced no words about it afterward.

THE ROOKIE BATEMAN PROVES A DUDE, AND THE CANADIANS TAKE ANOTHER: CANADIANS 5, HUB NINE 3

Brett Bateman, a rookie of very recent vintage, doubled home one run and singled home another, and Toronto — scrappy, stubborn, and suddenly warm — collected a second straight victory. Cease struck out seven in five innings without a decision, the fresh-summoned Chase Lee took the win (see the shuttle desk above), and Straw's insurance double preceded Miles' first save. Rafaela and Abreu homered in the Boston cause, and the debutant Rutschman reached three times (see the news column), but the Hub nine have now dropped four consecutive and feel every one of their nine games behind Tampa Bay.

THREE HITS SUFFICE WHERE SIX SCORELESS INNINGS LEAD: ATLANTAS 4, METROPOLITANS 0

The economy of it: Atlanta collected precisely three hits and won by four, for two of the three left the premises — Albies' twentieth and Olson's five-and-thirtieth, the latter drawing him level atop the game's home-run column (see the news desk). Martín Pérez supplied six scoreless innings for his eighth victory, extending a run of shutout work that has the wires talking rotation arithmetic in Atlanta, and three relievers finished the whitewash. McLean deserved kinder — six innings, one run — but the Metropolitans were blanked on four hits, and the Atlantas roll on at two-and-seventy wins.

THREE CIRCUITS IN THREE INNINGS AND THE BALTIMORES ARE OFF EARLY: BALTIMORES 5, NORTH STARS 2

The visitors wasted no ceremony upon Ober: Alonso's six-and-twentieth cleared the wall in the first with a man aboard — his seven-and-seventieth run driven in — Henderson's nineteenth followed in the second, likewise a two-run affair, and Encarnacion-Strand made it three homers in three innings in the third. Young rode the cushion to his ninth victory against three defeats, and Kittredge filed the sixth save. Minnesota, held to two, has lost seven of ten and slides in the wild-card queue.

ON POPE HAT NIGHT, PROVIDENCE WEARS CINCINNATI RED: REDLEGS 5, PALE HOSE 4, IN TEN INNINGS

Before a sellout of eight-and-thirty thousand crowned in papal headgear, Chicago built a four-nought lead on circuits by Doyle, Quero, and Vargas — his five-and-twentieth — with Antonacci's run-scoring double for good measure, and Burke of the home flannels struck out eight across seven fine innings. The visitors unraveled all of it: Suárez homered in the fifth, a three-run eighth arrived on De La Cruz's single and Stephenson's two-run blow, and in the tenth De La Cruz lifted the decisive sacrifice fly. A different Burke — Cincinnati's — took the victory, and Pagán, having won a fourteen-pitch war of attrition along the way, sealed his fourteenth save. The Pale Hose still lead the American's Central, but the cushion thins.

PALLANTE MATCHES THE ALL-STAR ZERO FOR ZERO, THEN HIS FRIENDS FINISH IT: MOUND CITY NINE 2, BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 0

Andre Pallante and Cristopher Sánchez — the latter owning the National's most victories at fifteen — traded six scoreless innings apiece, Sánchez striking out seven to no profit whatever. The decision fell upon the successors: Winn singled home Walker in the seventh off the same-day call-up McFarlane, Pereira added his fifth homer in the eighth, and O'Brien closed his thirtieth save, drawing level with San Diego's Miller atop the National's column. Philadelphia, blanked on five hits, thereby completes its descent into the three-way wild-card knot chronicled above.

THE HALOS ANSWER A HARD WEEK WITH A TIDY THIRD INNING: HALOS 3, LONE STAR NINE 2

All the home scoring arrived in one frame: Neto singled home a run, Schanuel lifted a sacrifice fly, and Grissom doubled home a third, undoing Pederson's two-and-twentieth homer from the first. Bradford pitched seven honest innings for Texas and was beaten anyway, though the fresh-arrived Kelenic singled home a run in the sixth (see the shuttle desk); Fermin took the decision and Natera Jr. the third save. The defeat stings in Arlington: with Houston also beaten, the Lone Star nine remain half a game out of first in the American's West, a rung they might have claimed outright.

KARROS TURNS ONE SWING AGAINST THE DESERT: MOUNTAIN MEN 3, SONORAN NINE 2

Arizona opened as if intent on a rout, Carroll and Marte homering in the game's first six batters, and then scored no more forever. Kyle Karros flattened the evening with a two-run circuit in the sixth — his tenth — and Moniak's sacrifice fly in the seventh completed the reversal. Sugano claimed his twelfth victory with six sturdy innings, Romano filed the eleventh save, and the Sonoran nine, thus upset by the National's rearmost club, awoke to find themselves sharing a wild-card berth with two housemates (see the day's principal dispatch).

WALLS WAITS A YEAR FOR ONE HOMER AND THIRTY MINUTES FOR THE NEXT: SUNSHINE NINE 12, MACKMEN 4

Taylor Walls had not homered in three hundred and eighty days; last night he did it twice inside half an hour, driving in three, and his fellows made the occasion general — Caminero's five-and-thirtieth (see the news column), Díaz's seventeenth, Mesa Jr.'s tenth, and the first circuit of young Carson Williams' major-league life, a three-run flourish in the eighth. Martinez pitched the whole nine innings for his twelfth victory against three defeats. Eight straight wins now for the Sunshine nine, three-and-seventy in sum, and the American's best account grows fatter by the evening; the Mackmen, for their part, have dropped eight of ten.

THE ROOKIE BATTERY CARRIES THE BAY: BAY NINE 4, HOUSTON NINE 1

Whisenhunt wriggled through five and two-thirds innings conceding but a single run, the rookie catcher Cavanaugh collected two hits, a run driven in, and his first stolen base, and Eldridge's twelfth homer supplied the exclamation as San Francisco held Houston to five hits. Peña committed two errors in a forgettable visitor's evening; Alvarez's sacrifice fly — his seven-and-eightieth run driven in, the American's most — was the whole of the Texan offense. Houston's hold on the American's West remains half a game, preserved only by Texas losing simultaneously down the coast.

SNELL STRIKES OUT TEN IN HIS RESURRECTION, AND MUNCY WALKS IT OFF ONCE MORE: ANGELENOS 5, MISSOURIANS 4, IN TEN INNINGS

Blake Snell, absent three months for the removal of loose bodies from his pitching elbow — his sharpening credited by the wires to a high-altitude rehabilitation start — returned with six innings of three-hit, ten-strikeout work before a crowd of nearly fifty thousand. The melodrama followed his exit: Kansas City struck thrice in the eighth against Phillips, Caglianone and Perez singling home runs before an error let in a third, and Betts — who had homered earlier, his fourteenth — leveled matters with a single in the bottom half. In the tenth, the bases full, Max Muncy singled home Ohtani for the second consecutive night of late-inning deliverance from his bat. Halvorsen took the victory, and the champions have quietly won two straight.

A full card of fifteen decorates this Wednesday, and the desk commends the following: at 2:15 the Brotherly Love nine seek their revenge in St. Louis behind Wheeler, ten-and-three with a 2.69 figure; at five past three the Sunshine nine send Rasmussen and his 2.75 against the Mackmen, nine straight in their sights; at ten past four the Brewers attempt to arrest their skid in San Diego with May opposing Ray; and the evening belongs to a pair of American League showdowns upon the national broadcast — the Puget Sound men at the Bronx at 7:05, and the Lone Star nine at Anaheim at ten past ten, half a game of first place riding on Texan shoulders. The sentimentalist is directed to Dyersville this afternoon for the High School All-Americans, and to the same corn upon the morrow, when the Twins and Phillies play the Field of Dreams game proper. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: EIGHT RUNS IN THE EIGHTH AND THE WHOLE LEDGER TURNS OVER: TAMPA MEN 10, WHITE ELEPHANTS 6
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 34 · Tuesday, the Eleventh of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 10 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

EIGHT RUNS IN THE EIGHTH AND THE WHOLE LEDGER TURNS OVER: TAMPA MEN 10, WHITE ELEPHANTS 6

Trailing by four with six outs left to spend, the American's finest club sends ten men to the plate in a single frame — Caminero's four-and-thirtieth circuit the thunderclap, Walls and Aranda the fine print — and a seventh consecutive victory is carried off from a night that had held a steal of home against them

Through seven innings the finest club in the American League had been made to look a very ordinary one. The White Elephants had pilfered a run in the boldest style the game allows — Tyler Soderstrom, having doubled home Jeff McNeil in the first, straightaway stole home while the Tampa men watched in disbelief — and Zack Gelof, restored from the sick list only that afternoon, celebrated his health with a homer in the fifth and a run-scoring double in a four-run seventh. At two runs against six, the arithmetic sat heavily against Tampa Bay.

Then came the eighth, and the eighth was a massacre. Junior Caminero opened the account with a three-run blow to left center — his four-and-thirtieth of the season, one shy of Alvarez of Houston atop the American's column — and the procession scarcely paused for breath thereafter: Chandler Simpson, he of the league's three-and-thirty stolen bases, singled home a run; Taylor Walls singled home two more; Yandy Díaz, whose sixteenth homer had opened the game's scoring seven innings prior, lifted a sacrifice fly; and Jonathan Aranda singled home the eighth tally of the frame. Ten men to the plate, eight runs across, and the unhappy Suarez — charged with four of them while recording but a single out — left holding both the blown save and the defeat. Roycroft, himself roughed for three in the seventh, was forgiven everything by the ledger and handed the victory.

The Gulf Coast club thus runs its streak to seven straight, stands two-and-seventy wins against six-and-forty defeats — the American's best account by six full games over New York — and shows no inclination whatever toward moderation. The Elephants, who had played a spirited game and even received an errorless-streak-keeper's double from Jacob Wilson, were left to reflect that against this opponent, seven good innings is presently two short of the requirement.

News Around the League

A WEEK'S HINDSIGHT UPON THE GREAT DEALINGS, AND THE CATCHER PRIZE REPORTS THIS VERY DAY

The wires, having caught their breath, devote a long column to the executives' own reckoning of the season's frenzied Trade Deadline, now one week gone — a market whose principal fruits are already on display nightly (the Cy Young man Skubal's first Dodger Stadium turn is chronicled upon the card below). And the last great prize comes off the shelf this very day: Boston is set to activate Adley Rutschman, the thrice-an-All-Star catcher obtained at the Deadline, in time for tonight's engagement at Toronto. The Crimson Hose, thrice beaten running, will not pretend the reinforcement arrives too soon.

THE INFIRMARY WARD SWELLS: WILLIAMS AND EOVALDI TO THE SHELF, TAILLON CARRIES HIS DEBUT OFF EARLY

A grim morning for the medical men. The Mets have placed their ninth-inning keeper Devin Williams upon the fifteen-day list with a strain of the right shoulder — the vacancy that handed Senga his first save, as the card below relates — and Texas has shelved Nathan Eovaldi, he of the ten victories, with inflammation of the right elbow. In Toronto, Jameson Taillon departed his Blue Jays debut after four one-hit innings with discomfort of the forearm, the club awaiting the examiners' verdict.

The ward offers brighter beds as well: Byron Buxton has taken batting practice upon the field and run the bases for the first time since his hip complaint, eyeing a weekend return to Minnesota's service, and Atlanta's Spencer Strider and Hurston Waldrep have both been cleared to begin throwing once more.

THE NINTH-INNING MARKET CHURNS: KIMBREL MADE OFFICIAL IN KANSAS CITY, SEWALD CAST OFF IN THE DESERT

The Kimbrel intelligence these pages carried yesterday is now a matter of record: Kansas City has formally activated Craig Kimbrel, nine times an All-Star, to its relief corps. Arizona, meanwhile, has conducted a wholesale rearrangement of its own late innings — designating Paul Sewald for assignment despite his four-and-twenty saves, among the National's leaders in that column, and signing the free agent Zack Littell, who repaid the ink on his contract the very same night with four and two-thirds scoreless innings and a victory (see the card below). The ninth inning, the Herald observes, is a profession of no tenure whatever.

A RELIEF ACE BY REINVENTION: THE SOUTH SIDERS' HICKS REMADE IN MIDSEASON

The wires examine a quiet marvel on Chicago's South Side, where Jordan Hicks has emerged — by way of a deliberate midseason overhaul of his craft — as something very like an ace of the relief corps. The timing could scarcely be better: the White Sox sit atop the American's Central, three and a half games to the good, and pennant arithmetic in September is chiefly a matter of who owns the late innings.

THE ALMANAC: OCTOBER'S TIMETABLE IS PUBLISHED, AND THE CORN AWAITS

The league has published its postseason schedule, and the connoisseur may now pencil October into the family calendar with dates attached. Nearer at hand, the minor leaguers take the Field of Dreams stage in the Iowa corn this very evening — St. Paul's men and the Cubs' farmhands the participants — as a prelude to Thursday, when the Twins and Phillies play the Field of Dreams game proper at Dyersville. The regular campaign's final day, the almanac desk notes for the record, falls upon the twenty-seventh of September.

The Rest of the Card

A FOURTH OUT FOR BOSTON, BUT THE BUFFALO EXPRESS DELIVERS FOR TORONTO: MAPLE LEAF NINE 2, CRIMSON HOSE 1

The oddity of the night: Boston's lone tally arrived in the seventh by way of the seldom-seen fourth-out rule, the umpires reviewing Rafaela's sacrifice double play and ruling that Seigler's run should stand — a technicality the rulebook scholars will be dining out on for a week. Toronto's answer was manpower fresh off the Buffalo train: Charles McAdoo, recalled only yesterday, struck his second major-league homer in the fifth, Giménez singled home Springer in the sixth, and Simeon Woods Richardson, likewise just summoned, spun one and two-thirds hitless innings for the victory after Taillon's early exit (see the infirmary column). Varland sealed his five-and-twentieth save, and Gray — the American's leader with fourteen victories — absorbed but his third defeat.

FIVE IN THE FIRST AND BATY WITH THE BASES FULL: FLUSHING NINE 8, TOMAHAWK NINE 5

The Mets settled the principal business before Atlanta had batted: five runs in the opening frame, crowned by Brett Baty's grand slam, his eighth circuit of the year. Lindor added his eleventh in the third and a sacrifice-fly run in the ninth for good measure, and when the Tomahawk nine had clawed within three, the final flourish belonged to Kodai Senga — pressed into the ninth by Williams' infirmity and rewarded with the first save of his major-league life. Duarte took his first victory in relief; Elder bore the defeat; and Atlanta's lead in the National's East is trimmed to seven and a half games over Philadelphia.

KREMER RETURNS TO VEX HIS OLD EMPLOYERS WITH SEVEN ONE-HIT INNINGS: TWIN CITIES NINE 9, BIRDS 5

Dean Kremer, lately of Baltimore and now in Minnesota flannels, gave his former club the unfriendliest of welcomes: one hit and one run across seven innings, seven strikeouts, and no sentiment whatever. His fellows supplied the margin in a five-run seventh — Jeffers singling home two before Josh Bell's three-run sixteenth — and Austin Martin had opened the account with his third homer. The Birds' late flurry, Coby Mayo driving home three of their five, arrived well after the verdict was in; Rogers took the loss, and the Twins have won two running.

PAINTER CARRIES A NO-HITTER INTO THE SIXTH: QUAKERS 6, REDBIRDS 5

The young Andrew Painter held St. Louis hitless into the sixth inning and finished with two hits and six strikeouts across five and a third — a work of art with an anxious postscript, for the Redbirds struck thrice in the eighth, Burleson driving home three of their five runs on the night. Philadelphia's cushion, built on Sosa's three runs driven in and Schwarber's run-scoring double, held by a single tally, and Bowlan recorded the first save of his major-league account. The Quakers, at four-and-sixty wins, keep their seat at the National's wild-card table.

TROUT'S TWENTIETH IS THE WHOLE OF THE SERAPHS' EVENING: ARLINGTON MEN 4, SERAPHS 1, IN TEN INNINGS

MacKenzie Gore, in his first start since welcoming a daughter into the world — and hours after his rotation-mate Eovaldi went to the shelf — struck out nine Angels across five and a third innings, conceding only Mike Trout's twentieth homer in the first. The game sat level at one until the tenth, when Nimmo singled home the go-ahead run and Jake Burger singled home two more; Gray took the victory to stand six-and-none, and Latz sealed his three-and-twentieth save. Texas thus draws within half a game of Houston in the American's West, while the Seraphs remain the division's rearmost tenant.

ARENADO CLEARS THE BASES BEFORE AN OUT IS RECORDED: SNAKES 9, MILE HIGH NINE 0

Nolan Arenado greeted his old mountain acquaintances with a grand slam in a four-run first — his eighteenth circuit — and Arizona piled on three more in the second by Carroll's four-and-twentieth double, a wild pitch, and Marte's single. The pitching told the quieter story: Soroka, back from the sick list, handed the game to Zack Littell, signed as a free agent only the day before, who threw four and two-thirds scoreless innings for the victory while Colorado managed five hits in sum. The Snakes have won two straight and sit level with Philadelphia at the National's wild-card table.

MERRILL MAKES IT THREE MORNINGS RUNNING: MISSION NINE 3, BREW CREW 2

Jackson Merrill struck his third homer in as many games — a two-run, go-ahead blow in the seventh, his nineteenth of the year — to overturn the two-run homer Yelich had struck in the second, the veteran answering his demotion in the batting order in the most eloquent style available. Ty France's seventeenth had kept San Diego within reach, Matsui took the decision, and Miller sealed his thirtieth save to stand alone atop the National's column. The Mission nine have won three straight; the Brew Crew, at four-and-seventy wins, remain owners of the game's finest ledger even in defeat.

DOWN TO A FINAL STRIKE, THEN THREE IN THE TENTH: 'STROS 6, BAY NINE 3, IN TEN INNINGS

San Francisco led by Jung Hoo Lee's ninth homer and Drew Gilbert's fifth, and had the visitors down to their final strike in the ninth — whereupon Cam Smith, whose sixteenth circuit had kept Houston breathing in the seventh, singled home the levelling run. In the tenth the 'Stros collected the whole account: Peña singled home the lead and Paredes doubled home two behind him, while Hader threw two hitless innings for the victory. Houston thereby preserves its half-game hold on the American's West, Texas breathing on its collar.

SKUBAL TAKES THE HOME HILL, MUNCY CLEARS THE BASES, AND THE BOYS IN BLUE EXHALE: DODGERS 6, ROYAL BLUES 5

Before one-and-fifty thousand at Chavez Ravine, Tarik Skubal made his first home start in Los Angeles flannels — five innings, three runs, six strikeouts, and an honest confession of nerves to the wires afterward. The evening's melodrama outlasted him: Caglianone struck his one-and-twentieth homer among three runs driven in for Kansas City, Muncy's bases-clearing double turned the game in a three-run sixth, Isbel levelled it with a two-run blow in the seventh, and Freeman singled home Ohtani — his second such delivery of the night — for the decisive run in the bottom half, accepting an out at second base as the price. Dreyer took the victory, Díaz the sixth save, and the champions, lately two-and-eight across their last ten, return home to find their division lead steadied at seven and a half games.

Ten contests decorate this Tuesday's card, and the desk commends the following to the connoisseur: at seven minutes past seven, Boston calls at Toronto with the catcher Rutschman's debut expected on the bill and Cease, he of the 2.28 figure, engaged for the Torontos; at 7:45 the Quakers open the evening in St. Louis behind Sánchez and his fifteen victories, the National's most, against Pallante and his twelve; at forty minutes past nine the Brew Crew visit the Mission nine with Harrison, nine-and-two, opposing Buehler, while the Tampa men — eight straight in their sights — send Martinez and his 2.65 against the Elephants; and at ten past ten Kansas City closes the night in Los Angeles once more. The sentimentalist is reminded that Thursday brings the Twins and Phillies to the Iowa corn at Dyersville for the Field of Dreams game, the minor leaguers rehearsing the stage this very evening. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO HUNDRED STRIKEOUTS FOR THE MIZ, AND A WALK-OFF BESIDES: SUDS MEN 4, NORTH STARS 3
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 33 · Monday, the Tenth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO HUNDRED STRIKEOUTS FOR THE MIZ, AND A WALK-OFF BESIDES: SUDS MEN 4, NORTH STARS 3

Misiorowski fans nine and crosses the two-hundred mark faster than all but one pitcher in the game's recorded history, the rookie Lara twice robs Minnesota by feats the wires can only call Spider-manning, and Bauers — a homer already to his name — singles home Turang in the tenth to settle it

Begin with the arithmetic, for it is the kind that gets a man remembered. Jacob Misiorowski struck out nine Minnesotans across six innings on Sunday, and somewhere in that harvest his season's account passed two hundred — a figure reached, the wires certify, faster than all but one pitcher in the whole recorded history of the game. His ledger now reads two hundred and four strikeouts and a 1.76 figure, both of them atop the National League by the width of a county, and the crowd in Milwaukee understood perfectly well what it was watching.

The game itself insisted on being interesting anyway. Jackson Chourio opened the account with his seventeenth circuit in the first; Brooks Lee answered with his seventeenth in the fifth; Jake Bauers restored the lead with his one-and-twentieth in the bottom half and David Hamilton doubled home Sánchez behind him; and Kody Clemens levelled the whole argument at three apiece with a two-run blow in the sixth. In between, the rookie Luis Lara twice went up the wall to rob Minnesota of extra bases — "all of a sudden he's Spider-manning," by the wires' awed account — and the relief corps of both clubs pitched blank frames until the tenth, when Bauers lined a single to left, Brice Turang raced home, and Hall collected his first victory of the year.

The Herald's almanac desk notes, with a raised eyebrow, that this is the second morning running these pages have set down Brewers 4, Twins 3 — the schedule occasionally repeats itself for emphasis. At four-and-seventy wins against four-and-forty defeats, Milwaukee's remains the finest ledger in all of baseball, five and a half games clear of Chicago in the National's Central.

News Around the League

THE CY YOUNG MAN CHANGES COASTS: SKUBAL, LATELY OF DETROIT, TAKES THE DODGER STADIUM HILL THIS VERY EVENING

The wires devote their largest type to Tarik Skubal, the two-time Cy Young laureate obtained from Detroit in the season's great dealings, who makes his first home start in Los Angeles flannels tonight against Kansas City at ten past ten Eastern. He arrives bearing a 2.81 figure — and arrives, it must be said, not a moment early: the Angelenos have dropped eight of their last ten and watched their division lead thin to seven and a half games (the desert's latest contribution to that misery is chronicled upon the card below).

ONE HUNDRED AND ELEVEN GAMES WITHOUT A MISPLAY: THE ATHLETICS' YOUNG SHORTSTOP RETIRES BORDICK'S RECORD

At Fenway Park this weekend, Jacob Wilson of the Athletics carried his errorless run at shortstop to one hundred and eleven consecutive games, passing the mark of Mike Bordick to stand alone in the annals — every chance accepted, every throw true, across better than two-thirds of a season's worth of afternoons. The wires pronounce it a record for the position, and the Herald pronounces it the quietest sort of greatness there is. His club, it happens, keeps noisy company with the feat: see the card below, where the Mackmen made it two straight over Boston.

NINE TIMES AN ALL-STAR AND BOUND FOR KANSAS CITY: KIMBREL REPORTED TO JOIN THE ROYALS' RELIEF CORPS

The wires carry word, by way of a source, that Craig Kimbrel — nine times an All-Star and among the most decorated ninth-inning men of his era — has been added by Kansas City to shore up a bullpen that has wanted for shoring. The Missourians' present standing (see their Sunday misfortune upon the card) suggests the veteran is engaged for dignity as much as for the pennant arithmetic, but a famous arm is a famous arm, and the Herald will report his first appearance in royal blue when it comes.

THE CATCHER'S LONG ROAD REACHES ITS LAST MILE: RUTSCHMAN EXPECTED IN BOSTON'S SERVICE AT TORONTO

Adley Rutschman, whose rehabilitation doings these pages chronicled only yesterday, is now on the cusp of his first game in Boston employ: the wires expect the thrice-an-All-Star catcher to make his debut during the series that opens this very evening in Toronto. The Hub nine, having dropped two straight since their nine-game procession ended, would receive him the way a parched man receives rain.

THE YOUNGEST LINEUP EVER ASSEMBLED IS ALSO THE MOST PRODUCTIVE: THE CAPITAL NINE LEAD ALL CREATION IN RUNS

The wires observe a marvel in Washington: the Nationals are fielding the youngest everyday lineup the game has ever recorded, and that same company of youths presently leads all thirty clubs in run production. Sunday the children completed their first sweep since April (the particulars sit upon the card below), behind an overhauled relief corps that has lately made a habit of blank innings. The Herald, which has watched Abrams and the prodigy Nuñez — he of the National's best forty stolen bases — all season, confesses no surprise, only admiration.

The Rest of the Card

SALE IS EJECTED BEFORE A PITCH IS THROWN, AND THE DUEL GOES TEN: ATLANTAS 2, PINSTRIPES 1

The afternoon's first casualty was Chris Sale, not engaged to pitch and expelled before the first pitch was thrown — Saturday's balk quarrel, evidently, being unfinished business. The game that followed was a jewel: Schlittler struck out eleven across seven innings for New York, Holmes answered with six scoreless frames, Olson's four-and-thirtieth circuit in the seventh was matched by Grisham's thirteenth in the eighth, and in the tenth Michael Harris II singled home Kim to spare Atlanta the sweep. Iglesias took the decision, Kinley his first save, and the Atlantas guard the National's East by eight and a half games.

HEIM LEVELS IT IN THE EIGHTH, MUNCY WINS IT IN THE NINTH: MACKMEN 4, HUB NINE 3

On the weekend of Wilson's record-keeping (see the news column), his club made it two straight at Fenway: Jonah Heim doubled home the levelling run off Whitlock in the eighth, and Max Muncy doubled home Walton off Chapman in the ninth, with Harris sealing his eleventh save. Ginn gave six innings of one-earned-run ball, and Boston — five and a half games clear yet in the wild-card ledger — has now lost two running since its nine-game streak perished.

TWELVE INNINGS, TWO SCHWARBER CIRCUITS, AND HILL DELIVERS THE VERDICT: PHILS 7, CANADIANS 6

Kyle Schwarber ended his brief homer famine emphatically — a three-run blow in the third and a solo in the fifth, his four-and-thirtieth and five-and-thirtieth, restoring him to the summit of the National's home-run column — and Luzardo struck out twelve across seven innings besides. Toronto clawed level by Giménez's two-run single in the eighth and nosed ahead in the twelfth, whereupon Philadelphia answered with two: Stott's single to level, and Derek Hill's single to end it. The Phils hold the wild-card line alongside Arizona, eight and a half behind Atlanta.

ELEVEN STRIKEOUTS FOR MANAEA AND FOUR RUNS DRIVEN BY ROBERT: AMAZINS 11, BUCS 1

One evening after being blanked on three singles, the Flushing men administered fifteen hits' worth of correction: Luis Robert Jr. drove home four with a circuit and a sacrifice fly, Bo Bichette struck a pair of doubles among three runs driven in, Alvarez added his thirteenth homer, and Sean Manaea struck out eleven Pittsburghers across seven innings of three-hit ball. Jones was charged with eight runs in three frames, and the Bucs have now surrendered twenty runs in two nights of this series.

CONINE TWICE, SANOJA THRICE, AND A SIX-RUN FIFTH: GULF STREAM NINE 12, HALOS 3

Griffin Conine struck two circuits, the eleventh and twelfth, and drove home three; Javier Sanoja singled home three more; and a six-run fifth turned a one-run affair into a rout. The Miami nine have won two straight and stand three games shy of the wild-card table at sixty wins — while the Halos, their evening's offense confined chiefly to Siri's seventh homer, remain the American West's rearmost tenant.

THE BROOM COMES OUT IN THE CAPITAL FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE APRIL: CAPITAL NINE 7, REDLEGS 1

The sweep the news column celebrates was completed without suspense: Dion, three innings of one-hit relief, took his first victory behind Ortiz's homer, and a three-run eighth crowned by Chaparro's two-run double put the matter beyond debate. Cincinnati managed a single tally and nine strikeouts against Washington's assembled youth, and the Redlegs' pursuit of the wild-card table has now lost three steps running.

EIGHTEEN HITS AND AN EIGHTH VICTORY AGAINST ONE DEFEAT FOR BOYD: NORTH SIDERS 10, MISSOURIANS 2

Matthew Boyd went seven workmanlike innings for an eight-and-one ledger while his fellows collected eighteen hits: Bregman singled home two, Happ struck a two-run twentieth, Amaya a three-run blow in a three-run seventh, and Hoerner kept the machinery turning throughout. The North Siders, at nine-and-sixty wins, hold the National's first wild-card chair by a comfortable six games — and the Kansas City nine, awaiting their famous new fireman (see the news column), were reminded why he was sent for.

TWO HITLESS INNINGS IN HIS FIRST HOUR AS A MAJOR LEAGUER: HAGEN SMITH WINS HIS DEBUT, SOUTH SIDERS 5, FOREST CITY NINE 3

The debutant Hagen Smith walked four men and allowed none of them a hit across two innings, and for his nerve was handed the victory when Colson Montgomery's three-run circuit — his six-and-twentieth, level with Murakami among the American's leaders — capped a four-run third. Richards survived a nervous ninth for his first save, the South Siders claimed the series from Cleveland, and their lead in the American's Central stands at three and a half games over Detroit.

GOODMAN'S FOUR-AND-THIRTIETH IS ANSWERED INSIDE THE HALF-HOUR: MOUND CITY NINE 7, ROX 4

Hunter Goodman levelled the game at four apiece with his four-and-thirtieth homer in the eighth, and St. Louis replied with three in the bottom half — Wetherholt's two-run double the decisive blow, Herrera singling home the third. Burleson had earlier struck his nineteenth, O'Brien sealed his nine-and-twentieth save to stand level with San Diego's Miller atop the National's column, and the Cardinals return to the even mark of nine-and-fifty wins apiece, three and a half from the wild-card table.

ALONSO STRIKES TWO IN AN ORIOLE UNIFORM FOR THE FIRST TIME: BALTIMORES 10, LONE STAR NINE 5

Pete Alonso struck his four-and-twentieth and five-and-twentieth circuits — his first two-homer afternoon in Baltimore colors, the wires note — and drove home four, while Cowser and O'Neill added blows of their own and Rocker was excused after three innings and six runs. The defeat returns Texas to the exact even mark of nine-and-fifty wins and as many losses, half a game behind Houston in the West and clinging to the American's final wild-card chair with Detroit a single game astern.

WEBB'S EIGHT FINE INNINGS ARE BURIED IN THE TENTH: MOTOR CITY NINE 3, JINTS 1

Logan Webb allowed one run across eight innings and got nothing for it: in the tenth, Hao-Yu Lee singled home Greene and Max Clark's force-out fetched a third run, while Detroit's relief corps — Jansen striking out three in the tenth for the victory, Holton three more in the bottom half for the save — barred every door. The Bengals of yesterday's dispatch, now the Motor City nine of today's, have won two straight, and head home from their western journey one game shy of the wild-card table.

RODRIGUEZ SPENDS ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTEEN PITCHES AND BUYS A SEASON SERIES: DESERT NINE 4, ANGELENOS 2

Ketel Marte's twentieth circuit put Arizona two runs to the good before an out was recorded, and Eduardo Rodriguez did the rest — seven innings, nine strikeouts, one hundred and fifteen pitches, an eleventh victory against four defeats — in a duel of eleven-and-four men wherein Wrobleski blinked first. The wires observe that the Desert nine have thus secured the season's series from Los Angeles for the first time since eighteen, and the champions' division lead is pared to seven and a half games — with their new ace's answer scheduled for this very evening (see the news column).

A BROOM IN SEATTLE, A SIXTH STRAIGHT VICTORY, AND FOUR HITS FROM THE THIRD CHAIR: SUNSHINE NINE 4, M'S 1

Promoted to third in the batting order, the fleet Chandler Simpson answered with four hits, and Liam Hicks' two-run double crowned a fourteen-hit afternoon behind Seymour's seven-strikeout work. The Sunshine nine thus complete the sweep, run their streak to six, and hold the American's finest ledger at one-and-seventy wins — while Seattle, four defeats running, watches the wild-card table recede.

FOUR CIRCUITS, ONE FROM THE NEWEST MAN IN HIS FIRST TIME AT BAT: FRIARS 7, HOUSTON NINE 2

San Diego answered Varsho's early two-run homer with four of their own: Merrill's eighteenth, Tatis Jr.'s three-run eleventh, Sheets' fifteenth, and — the flourish — a blow from Austin Hays in his first time at bat since signing on, by the wires' delighted account. Vásquez held Houston to two hits over five innings, the Friars have won two straight to draw within one game of the wild-card line, and the Houston nine's grip on the American West is down to half a game over Texas.

Ten games adorn this Monday's card, and the connoisseur should arrange the evening thus: at seven minutes past seven, Boston opens in Toronto behind Gray and his fourteen-and-two ledger, the American's most victories — with the catcher Rutschman's debut in new colors possibly on the same bill; at a quarter past seven the Metropolitans call upon Atlanta; at 7:45 the Phillies open in St. Louis; at forty past nine the Brewers, owners of the game's best record, open in San Diego against the surging Friars, Henderson and his 2.70 against Mize; and at ten past ten the night closes upon Skubal's first Dodger Stadium start in Los Angeles flannels, Kansas City the visitor. The sentimentalist is reminded once more of Thursday, when the Twins and Phillies repair to the Iowa corn at Dyersville for the Field of Dreams game. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
